# Space-native construction materials for earth-independent and sustainable infrastructure

**M.Z. Naser**
*Glenn Department of Civil Engineering, Clemson University, Clemson, SC, 29634, USA*

## Abstract
A successful space exploration requires establishing permanent and earth-independent infrastructure that are not only resilient to the extreme environment of space but also preferably made of sustainable and indigenous “space-native” construction materials. This review covers feasibility of exploiting in-situ lunar and Martian resources as well as harvesting of elements and compounds, from near Earth objects (NEOs), to produce extraterrestrial materials suitable for construction of space-based infrastructure.

## 1. Introduction
Migration to the Moon or Mars is highly dependent upon development of resilient, economical, and sustainable infrastructure. Transportation costs range between $5000 to $20,000 per kg to the Moon. Utilizing in-situ resources (ISRU) could reduce the overall cost of a human settlement from $100 billion to an average of $40 billion.

### Table 1: Selected differences between Earth, Moon, and Mars
| Parameter | Earth | Moon | Mars |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Total mass compared to Earth (%) | 1.0 | 1.2 | 10.7 |
| Day duration (hrs) | 23.9 | 655.7 | 24.7 |
| Average surface temperature (ºC) | 13 | −30 | −57 |
| Atmospheric pressure (kPa) | 101.3 | negligible | 0.7 |

## 2. Space environment and resources
Space environments differ from Earth due to radiation (solar/galactic), vacuum, and low gravity. The lack of atmosphere on the Moon/Mars increases the impact effect of space debris (meteorites).

### 2.2.1 In-situ resource utilization (ISRU)
Regolith (fine particles covering the surface) can be processed into construction materials. Lunar and Martian regolith contain silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$), alumina ($Al_2O_3$), sulfur (S), and iron (FeO).

### Table 2: Chemical compositions (wt.%) of Martian and lunar soil samples
| Constituent | Lunar sample (Apollo 12) | Lunar sample (Apollo 17) | Martian sample (Chryse Planitia) | Cement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $SiO_2$ | 45.03 | 37.79 | 44.7 | 20.13 |
| $Al_2O_3$ | 21.09 | 19.66 | – | – |
| $FeO$ | 16.45 | 8.44 | 8.3 | 1.19 |
| $CaO$ | 2.54 | 12.97 | 0.9 | 0.37 |

## 3. Properties of space-native construction materials

### 3.1 Concrete-like hybrids
*   **Sulfur Concrete:** Water-free, created by heating sulfur (120–150 °C) and mixing with regolith. Compressive strengths reach 39–75.7 MPa.
*   **Polymer Concrete:** Uses polymeric resin binders. Strengths vary from 17 to 60 MPa.
*   **Geopolymers:** Formed by the interaction between aluminosilicate and an alkaline solution. Compressive strengths of 16.6–33.1 MPa.

### Table 4: Properties of lunar and Martian concrete
| Property | Lunar concrete | Martian concrete |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Compressive strength (MPa) | 39–75.7 | 20–63 |
| Tensile Strength (MPa) | 8.3 | 2.7–3.6 |
| Density ($kg/m^3$) | 2600 | – |

### 3.2 Metals and alloys
Lunar highlands contain ~15% aluminum oxide. Magnesium is found in olivine. These can be used to produce aluminum, magnesium, iron, and titanium structural components.

### Table 6: Properties of various metal alloys
| Property | 2014-T6 | 8090-T8771 | ZCM711 | Ti6Al4V | Beryllium Alloy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Ultimate strength (MPa) | – | 441.3 | 275 | 925 | 307 |
| Yield strength (MPa) | 410 | 344.8 | 185 | 860 | 222 |
| Young's modulus (GPa) | 72.5 | 80.7 | 45 | 108.5 | 303 |

## 4. Design considerations
Structures on the Moon and Mars can carry 3 to 6 times the mass on Earth due to low gravity, allowing for larger spans and thinner members. Foundations must be placed below the depth of thermal cycling to avoid settlement issues. Shielding (1–6 m of regolith) is proposed to protect against radiation and micrometeorites.

## 6. Summary and conclusions
*   ISRU eludes to the possibility of producing cementitious materials.
*   Water-free construction (sulfur, polymer) is essential.
*   Sustainable infrastructure can be fabricated with minimal Earth-based materials.
papers.keyFindings: Lunar and Martian regolith can be effectively transformed into construction materials such as sulfur concrete and geopolymers, which achieve compressive strengths comparable to Earth-based concrete (up to 75.7 MPa). The study identifies that the lower gravitational forces on these bodies (17-38% of Earth's) allow for more efficient structural designs with larger spans and thinner load-bearing members. Utilizing in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) for habitat construction could potentially reduce the cost of space settlements by approximately 60% compared to transporting all materials from Earth.
papers.findings: Feasibility study of space-native materials including regolith-based concretes (sulfur, polymer, geopolymer) and indigenous metals/alloys from the Moon, Mars, and NEOs. The paper reviews the effects of extreme vacuum, temperature fluctuations, and radiation on material performance and structural design for sustainable space infrastructure.
papers.result: Sulfur concrete demonstrated compressive strengths of 39–75.7 MPa (Lunar) and 20–63 MPa (Martian). Cast regolith achieved a compressive strength of 538 MPa and a tensile strength of 34.5 MPa. ISRU is estimated to reduce the cost of a human settlement from an average of $100 billion to $40 billion.

papers.relevanceReason: The paper presents the development of a 3D printing process for lunar regolith using concentrated solar sintering, which is a core technology for ISRU-based space habitat construction.

# Solar 3D printing of lunar regolith

**Authors:** A. Meurisse, A. Makaya, C. Willsch, M. Sperl  
**Journal:** Acta Astronautica 152 (2018) 800–810  
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.actaastro.2018.06.063

## Abstract
The authors demonstrated the feasibility of sintering lunar regolith layer-by-layer solely using concentrated sunlight. First trials using actual concentrated sunlight led to an inhomogeneous sintering of individual layers of lunar regolith simulant, due to the significant flux density variations caused by atmospheric fluctuations. Tests focusing Xenon light demonstrated however the concept with the manufacturing of the first solar 3D printed brick made of lunar regolith simulant. Actual compressive strength of the sintered bricks, below 5 MPa, might be currently too low for a direct lunar application. High porosity levels and weak layer-to-layer bonding were observed on the micro-scale, but ways of improving the technology were found by reducing the thermal gradient and the cooling time between consecutive layers. Adaptation of the technology on the Moon is presented to illustrate the suitability of solar additive manufacturing on the lunar surface, as a possible technique for shielding habitats and building roads prior to arrival of the astronauts.

## 1. Introduction
In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) can be used to reduce the risk and the cost of lunar missions. Building elements from lunar soil can create roads, launchpads, and habitat shelters. This paper combines concentrated sunlight with a 3D printing process to create the first 3D printer capable of creating 3D objects made of lunar regolith simulant sintered layer by layer.

## 2. Experimental Set-up
Sintering experiments were performed at the solar furnace facility of DLR-Köln. The High-Flux Solar Furnace consists of a 52 m² flat mirror (heliostat) reflecting light onto a concentrator. Experiments using Xenon light were carried out with the Xenon High-Flux Solar Simulator providing a power of 21 kW with a flux density of 4.3 MW/m². A 3-axis table was used to move a testbed under the concentrated solar beam, and a powder deposition system synchronized with the table dropped off each new layer (0.1 mm thickness).

## 3. Materials
JSC-1A and JSC-2A mare soil simulants were used. They are primarily composed of anorthite feldspath, plagioclase, pyroxene, and olivine minerals.

### Table 1: Lunar simulant composition (wt.%)
| Oxide | JSC-1A/JSC-2A | Lunar soil 14163 |
|---|---|---|
| SiO2 | 46,67 | 47,3 |
| TiO2 | 1,71 | 1,6 |
| Al2O3 | 15,79 | 17,8 |
| Fe2O3 | 3,41 | / |
| FeO | 7,57 | 10,5 |
| MgO | 9,39 | 9,6 |
| CaO | 9,90 | 11,4 |
| Na2O | 2,83 | 0,7 |
| K2O | 0,78 | 0,6 |
| MnO | 0,19 | 0,1 |
| P2O5 | 0,66 | / |

## 4. Solar Additive Manufacturing
- **Solar Sintering:** Initial tests showed that atmospheric fluctuations on Earth make actual solar sintering difficult for layered manufacturing. 
- **Solar Simulator:** Xenon lamps provided stable conditions. A 5-mm-thick 3D printed part was produced in 30 minutes, and a larger brick (240 x 120 mm) was produced in 3 hours 45 minutes.

## 5. Analysis and Discussion
Mechanical testing of sintered bricks showed a compression strength of 2.31 ± 0.30 MPa. Tomography revealed high porosity (open pores up to 0.60 mm). The weak bonding between layers is attributed to the thermal gradient and fast cooling on the edges. Vacuum environments on the moon are expected to improve mechanical properties by reducing oxidation and enhancing heat distribution through the absence of convection.

### Table 2: Compression test results
| Material | Compression strength (MPa) | Young's Modulus (GPa) |
|---|---|---|
| Solar 3D printed regolith | 2.31 ± 0.30 | 0.14 ± 0.06 |

## 6. Lunar Application
Solar 3D printing is envisioned for precursor missions to build infrastructure like shielding or roads. It could be implemented via heliostats reflecting light onto fixed tables or via mobile rovers with Fresnel lenses building directly on the surface.

## 7. Conclusion
The feasibility of 3D printing lunar regolith using concentrated solar light was demonstrated. While strength remains low for structural loads, it is suitable for protective shielding. Future work will focus on vacuum sintering and reducing thermal stress to improve interlayer bonding.
papers.keyFindings: The study successfully demonstrated the first 3D printing of lunar regolith bricks using concentrated solar energy in a layer-by-layer sintering process. Although the resulting material exhibits low compressive strength (~2.3 MPa) and high porosity, it is identified as a viable method for creating non-structural lunar infrastructure such as radiation shielding and roads.
papers.findings: Concentrated solar energy can be used to sinter lunar regolith into complex 3D shapes without additional binders. Atmospheric interference on Earth necessitates the use of solar simulators for stable process development, and the research identified high thermal gradients and rapid cooling as primary causes for weak interlayer bonding.
papers.result: The 3D printed regolith samples achieved a compressive strength of 2.31 ± 0.30 MPa and a Young's Modulus of 0.14 ± 0.06 GPa using 0.1 mm layer thickness and a fabrication time of approximately 3 hours 45 minutes for a 240 mm wide brick.

# A review towards the design of extraterrestrial structures: From regolith to human outposts

## Abstract
The design of a permanent human habitat on a planetary body other than the Earth is an idea introduced many decades ago... The scope of this paper is to present a meticulous selection of the most significant publications within the scientific areas related to: (a) geotechnical engineering aspects... (b) ground motions generated by different types of Moonquakes and meteoroid impacts; (c) the different concepts and types of extraterrestrial (ET) structures (generic, inflatable, deployable, 3D-printed), as well as overall views of proposed ET habitats.

## 1. Introduction
The 'space age' began in 1957. Civil engineering must now expand toward the construction of Lunar and Martian structures. Key environmental challenges include low gravity, temperature fluctuations, radiation, lack of atmosphere, and meteoroid impacts.

## 2. Aspects of Geotechnical Engineering
### 2.1. Lunar Regolith
Regolith density increases abruptly between 10 and 20 cm depth. 

**Table 1: Lunar soil density according to depth range [27].**
| Depth range (cm) | Bulk density, ρ (g/cm³) | Relative density, DR (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 0–15 | 1.50 ± 0.05 | 65 ± 3 |
| 0–30 | 1.58 ± 0.05 | 74 ± 3 |
| 30–60 | 1.74 ± 0.05 | 92 ± 3 |
| 0–60 | 1.66 ± 0.05 | 83 ± 3 |

### 2.2. Martian Regolith
Martian regolith is a mix of weathered and windblown material. The upper 5m layer is mainly cohesionless basaltic sand and rocks. Estimates suggest a minimum cohesion of 1–2 kPa based on slope stability back-analyses from InSight pits.

## 2.4. Anchoring in Regolith
Anchoring is essential for modular structures in microgravity to prevent potential uplifting. Methods reviewed include helical anchoring, suction drilling, circular wedge anchoring, and claw anchoring.

## 2.5. Regolith-based Landing Pads
Landing pads mitigate dust and plume effects. Materials reviewed include Lunar concrete (KOHLS-1), basalt pavers, and sintered regolith tiles using Contour Crafting or interlocking systems.

## 4. Extraterrestrial Structures
### 4.1. Generic Structural Concepts
Includes trusses supporting regolith shields (Benaroya), cable systems (Ettouney), and tensegrity structures.

### 4.2. Inflatable Structures
Inflatables are favored for their high volume-to-mass ratio and internal pressure resistance. Examples include TransHab and the Astrophytum concept.

### 4.3. Deployable Structures
Utilizing integral folding hinges (IFH) or origami-inspired designs for compact stowage during transport.

### 4.4. 3D-printed ET Structures
Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies include:
* **Selective Laser/Solar/Microwave Sintering:** Fusing regolith particles using heat.
* **Contour Crafting:** Extrusion-based layering of regolith mixed with binders (e.g., sulfur concrete).
* **D-shape:** Binder jetting methodology using regolith simulants.

## 6. Discussion
The review highlights that while regolith cohesion is low (<6 kPa), the internal friction angle is significant (>40°), facilitating foundation load transfer. Design evolution has moved from rigid Earth-made modules to hybrid inflatable-ISRU structures and finally to fully 3D-printed habitats utilizing microwave sintering.
papers.keyFindings: The paper identifies geotechnical properties, specifically the friction angle of regolith, as critical for foundation stability. It concludes that microwave sintering is the most promising ISRU-based additive manufacturing technique due to better heat penetration compared to solar or laser sintering. Additionally, hybrid structures combining inflatable pressurized volumes with 3D-printed regolith shielding are noted as the current leading design paradigm.
papers.findings: A high-level synthesis of extraterrestrial structural engineering, categorizing habitats into three classes (Class I-III) and summarizing the evolution of design from the Apollo era to modern automated construction concepts using in-situ resources.
papers.result: Compiles extensive data tables on regolith simulants (JSC-1, FJS, MLS-1, etc.), chemical compositions of Lunar vs. Martian soil, and mechanical performance of various foundation anchoring techniques (helical, suction, claw).

papers.title: Topological design of a new family of legged mobile landers based on Truss-Mechanism Transformation method
papers.relevanceReason: The paper discusses the topological design of legged mobile landers specifically intended for extraterrestrial base construction missions on the Moon and Mars, addressing automated construction and structural design requirements for space habitats.
papers.markdownContent:
# Topological design of a new family of legged mobile landers based on Truss-Mechanism Transformation method

## Abstract
To meet the needs of the 'Returning' and 'Base construction' missions of the extraterrestrial body's exploration task, it is necessary to enable the legged stationary lander (LSL) to walk. This paper proposes a novel synthesis method based on Truss-Mechanism Transformation (TMT method) for Legged Mobile Landers (LMLs) with capabilities of trusses and mechanisms during different phases.

## 1. Introduction
Deep space exploration mainly includes 'Circling', 'Landing', and 'Returning' missions, with 'Base construction' as a mission for the future. LSLs have advantages in stability and payload capacity but limited exploration range. The proposal of LMLs can meet requirements for large area exploration and base construction. One of the biggest issues is the degree of freedom (DoF) contradiction: landing requires a rigid truss (0 DoF), while walking requires a multi-DoF mechanism.

## 2. Overall topological design concept
A novel LML should accomplish five functions: 
- Being deployable
- Landing buffer
- Walking
- Orientation adjustment
- Terrain adaptability

## 3. TMT method for topological design
The method involves four stages:
1. Get motion requirements from functions.
2. Design trusses based on polyhedrons (Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2).
3. Design mechanism by allocating motions into the truss.
4. Type evaluation based on overconstraints and joint locations.

## 4. Innovative design of legs
The structure of Chang'e lander (V=6, E=9, F=5) is used as a base. The leg consists of an upper parallel structure (3 translations/mid-platform) and a lower terrain adaptability part (passive S joint). Four motion submanifolds are chosen for designing the legs, including rotation and translation combinations.

## 5. Two typical LMLs analyses
- **Case I**: UP&2-RUS with transmission limbs. The transmission limb protects actuators from impact forces during landing.
- **Case III**: RU&2-RUS with electromagnetic bolts. Actuators are protected by fixing RU links during landing.
Both cases allow 6-D mobility for walking and orientation adjustment.

## 6. Conclusion
The TMT method provides a new approach for designing robots with multiple functions (landing/walking). Four novel LMLs were obtained which can extend the range of exploration and support deep space base construction.
papers.keyFindings: The study introduces the Truss-Mechanism Transformation (TMT) method to design Legged Mobile Landers that function as rigid trusses during landing and multi-DoF robots for walking. These designs resolve the degree-of-freedom contradiction between stable landing and mobile base construction, facilitating improved exploration and habitat site preparation.
papers.findings: Developed the TMT (Truss-Mechanism Transformation) topological synthesis method for extraterrestrial landers, enabling a single structure to serve as both a high-load truss and a mobile mechanism.
papers.result: Synthesized four novel legged mobile lander leg structures based on the Chang'e lander topology, achieving zero overconstraints (Delta = 0) and providing 6-D mobility for surface walking and orientation adjustment.

papers.title: Ultrasonic tool for the realization of combined action during the drilling of extraterrestrial objects
papers.relevanceReason: The paper discusses the development of an ultrasonic drilling tool for extraterrestrial soil sampling and anchoring on low-gravity objects like asteroids and planets. This is critical for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) and geotechnical engineering for space habitats.
papers.markdownContent:
# Ultrasonic tool for the realization of combined action during the drilling of extraterrestrial objects

**Authors:** Vladimir N Khmelev, Roman V Barsukov, Viktor A Nesterov, Dmitry V Genne, Qiquan Quan and Roman N Golykh
**Journal:** Journal of Physics: Conference Series, 1679 (2020) 042033
**DOI:** 10.1088/1742-6596/1679/4/042033

## Abstract
The article is devoted to the problem of the efficiency increase of ultrasonic drilling of hard materials for the studies of the soils of the planets, asteroids and other space objects. It is proposed the solution of the problem by the help of developed device, which is able to realize simultaneously with ultrasound the action by low-frequency macro-oscillations and rotational motion of the leading edge of the tool. The tests of the practical construction of the developed device showed the possibility of the speed increase of the ultrasonic drilling due to the additional low-frequency oscillations and pseudo-rotation in up to 1.5 times.

## 1. Introduction
Drilling on extraterrestrial objects (planets, comets, asteroids) is essential for chemical analysis and finding life forms. On small bodies with low gravitation, traditional rotary drilling is impractical due to the high clamping force required and excessive heat generation, which can volatilize water and low-melting materials. Ultrasonic drilling is proposed as an alternative as it requires low pressing force, excludes heating, and can handle various materials.

## 2. Construction Description
The developed device combines ultrasonic drilling with shock low-frequency oscillations and rotational motion. The tool consists of a piezoelectric transducer (20 kHz), a concentrator, and a tubular working tool. Low-frequency oscillations (approx. 20 Hz) are generated by a loading mass that rebounds from the oscillating part of the concentrator. A pseudo-rotational drive provides periodic motion to the entire construction.

## 3. Results of the experiments
Tests were conducted using silicate brick, red construction brick, and foam concrete building blocks as samples. 

### Table 1. Main parameters of the ultrasonic working tool and its pseudo-rotation system.
| Parameter | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Amplitude of oscillations of the leading edge of the working tool, µm | 70 |
| Pressing force of ultrasonic working tool to the sample, N | 5, 10, 20 |
| Rotation angle of pseudo-rotation system, degree | 100 |
| Frequency of pseudo-rotational motion, Hz | 1 |
| Frequency of low-frequency oscillating motion, Hz | 20 |
| Pressing force of the loading mass to oscillating surface, N | 12 |

### Table 2. Silicate brick. Results of the drilling (speed in mm/min).
| Pressure (N) | RD | UD | UD+RD | UD+LFV | UD+LFV+RD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 | 4 | 27 | 30 | 30 | 42 |
| 10 | 2 | 16 | 17 | 18 | 24 |

### Table 3. Red brick. Results of the drilling (speed in mm/min).
| Pressure (N) | RD | UD | UD+RD | UD+LFV | UD+LFV+RD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 | 3 | 9 | 11 | 10 | 13 |
| 10 | 1 | 14 | 14 | 15 | 17 |
| 5 | 1 | 13 | 13 | 14 | 18 |

### Table 4. Foam concrete. Results of the drilling (speed in mm/min).
| Pressure (N) | RD | UD | UD+RD | UD+LFV | UD+LFV+RD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 | 11 | 122 | 134 | 136 | 154 |
| 10 | 10 | 91 | 102 | 100 | 136 |
| 5 | 5 | 55 | 59 | 60 | 102 |

*(Note: RD=Rotation, UD=Ultrasound, LFV=Low-Frequency Vibration)*

## 4. Conclusion
The study proved that combined action (UD+LFV+RD) increases drilling speed by approximately 49% (1.5 times) compared to pure ultrasonic drilling and 3-10 times compared to traditional rotation. The system allows for continuous control of electric parameters to define soil characteristics during drilling without separating the tool from the oscillating system.
papers.keyFindings: The integration of low-frequency oscillations and pseudo-rotation with ultrasonic drilling increases penetration rates by up to 1.5 times in brittle materials. This combined mechanism is highly suitable for low-gravity extraterrestrial environments as it requires minimal clamping force and prevents thermal degradation of samples.
papers.findings: Investigation into an enhanced ultrasonic drilling mechanism for extraterrestrial soil sampling that incorporates three modes of action: high-frequency ultrasound, low-frequency macro-oscillations, and pseudo-rotation.
papers.result: Drilling speed in silicate brick at 20N pressure reached 42 mm/min using combined action (UD+LFV+RD) compared to 27 mm/min for ultrasound alone and 4 mm/min for traditional rotation.

# Mechanical behavior of the metal parts welded with extraterrestrial regolith simulant by the solar concentrator in ISRU & ISRF application

**Authors:** Wei Zheng, Guofu Qiao
**Published in:** Advances in Space Research 65 (2020) 2303–2314
**Received:** 29 October 2019; **Accepted:** 9 February 2020

## Abstract
The use of in-situ resources plays an important role on future extraterrestrial human activities for the facility repair and habitat construction, especially in sustainable space exploration of Moon and Mars. A method of the metal welded with extraterrestrial regolith simulant using solar processing under ambient conditions is presented. Metal parts are made of Q235B ferroalloy and TA2 titanium alloy into standard tensile members according to the ASTM code. They are disconnected from the middle in advance, and then welded together with lunar and Martian regolith simulant under ambient conditions, respectively. The entire welding process and precautions are detailed. The results show that it is possible to weld metal parts together with extraterrestrial regolith simulant by the solar concentrator. 

## 1. Introduction
The long-term explorations of the Moon and Mars require mission sustainment and a steady supply of resources. In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) and in-situ fabrication and repair (ISFR) technologies can significantly reduce the required launch mass and cost. This research focuses on using solar energy as a heat resource to fabricate building elements and repair components using abundant basaltic-formed regolith.

## 2. Experimental

### 2.1 Materials
#### 2.1.1 Extraterrestrial regolith simulant
Two simulants were used:
- **HIT-L-1:** Harbin Institute of Technology Lunar Simulant 1.
- **HIT-M-1:** Harbin Institute of Technology Martian Simulant 1.

| Chemical Component | Apollo 14 | HIT-L-1 | RN bulk | HIT-M-1 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| SiO2 | 48.1 | 39.16 | 43.0 | 43.20 |
| Al2O3 | 17.4 | 13.41 | 9.4 | 15.29 |
| CaO | 10.7 | 17.10 | 7.3 | 9.87 |
| FeOt | 10.4 | 17.81 | 19.2 | 18.50 |
| MgO | 9.4 | 2.45 | 8.7 | 2.82 |
| TiO2 | 1.7 | 3.25 | 1.2 | 3.17 |
| SUM | 99.6 | 99.21 | 100.1 | 99.34 |

#### 2.1.2 Metal parts
- **Q235B Carbon Steel (Ferroalloy):** Yield strength 235 MPa, UTS 453 MPa.
- **TA2 Titanium Alloy:** Yield strength 373 MPa, UTS 516 MPa.

### 2.2 Welding Process
A Fresnel lens (450 mm diameter) was used to concentrate solar energy. The average heat flux density at the focal spot was approximately 56.5 MW/m².
1. A layer of regolith (~50 mg) was placed between two metal halves.
2. The Fresnel lens concentrated light to form a weld pool.
3. The focal spot moved along the interface to fuse the parts.
4. Weldments were buried in a powder bed to ensure slow cooling and minimize brittle failure.

## 3. Results and Discussion

| Specimen Type | Avg. Ultimate Tensile Strength (MPa) | Strength Ratio to Base Metal (%) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fe-Lunar (Fe-L) | 2.94 | 1.25% |
| Fe-Martian (Fe-M) | 1.66 | 0.71% |
| Ti-Lunar (Ti-L) | 4.95 | 1.33% |
| Ti-Martian (Ti-M) | 2.59 | 0.69% |

**Failure Mode:** All specimens exhibited brittle failure. Titanium alloys showed higher joint strength than ferroalloys when using the same regolith simulant. 

## 4. Conclusions
The study demonstrates the feasibility of welding metal parts with extraterrestrial regolith simulant using a solar concentrator. While current joint strengths are low (less than 2% of the base metal), the method provides a binderless path for ISRU-based fabrication and repair. The strength derives from oxygenated compounds fusing into the metal base at high temperatures.
papers.keyFindings: Solar energy concentrated via a Fresnel lens can successfully weld ferroalloy and titanium parts using regolith simulant as a solder. Titanium joints demonstrated higher ultimate tensile strength compared to ferroalloy joints, though all specimens exhibited brittle failure modes. The joint strength is attributed to the uniform fusion of wustite and silicate melts into the metal interface.
papers.findings: A novel ISRU welding method using solar thermal energy and regolith simulant as solder was experimentally verified. The study characterized the chemical composition and mechanical performance of the resulting joints for both lunar and Martian environmental simulants. Microstructural analysis via SEM/EDS revealed that the regolith fuses homogeneously into ferroalloys and inhomogeneously into titanium alloys, forming brittle oxygenated compounds.
papers.result: The average ultimate tensile strengths were 2.94 MPa (Fe-Lunar), 1.66 MPa (Fe-Martian), 4.95 MPa (Ti-Lunar), and 2.59 MPa (Ti-Martian). All joints achieved less than 2% of the base metal's original tensile strength, indicating a need for process optimization to improve structural integrity.

papers.title: A Framework for Extraterrestrial Environmental Assessment
papers.relevanceReason: The paper provides a framework for evaluating environmental impacts of space-based construction, mining, and habitation. It specifically addresses sustainability and management of ISRU activities on the Moon and Mars, which are core to space architecture planning.
papers.markdownContent:
# A Framework for Extraterrestrial Environmental Assessment

**William R. Kramer**
*Outer Space Consulting, Frederick, MD, 21701, USA*

## Abstract
Many proposed activities on the Moon, Mars, and elsewhere in our solar system require construction and mining. These actions alter natural environments, potentially foreclosing future options for use, hindering resource access, or harming scientific research. This article proposes a simple framework for **Extraterrestrial Environmental Assessment (EEA)** as a starting point for discussion, drawing on elements of Earth-based assessments but tailored for the unique challenges of space development.

## 1. A rapidly evolving problem in space development
Foreseeable physical activities on celestial bodies—such as construction, mining, energy production, and human habitation—may adversely affect extraterrestrial environments. Impacts include:
- Increased long-range costs and reduced efficiency.
- Interference with scientific research.
- Decreased human health and safety.
- Permanent alterations to alien landscapes (unlike Earth, these environments lack resilient tectonic/vegetative cycles).

## 2. The neglected need for extraterrestrial environmental assessment
Space actors have largely ignored environmental impacts. Potential conflicts include:
- **Resource Squandering:** "First in time" ventures may target the easiest-to-mine resources at the expense of long-term sustainability (e.g., water ice).
- **Physical Interference:** Blasting vibrations could invalidate seismic studies; dust from mining could coat solar panels or telescopes.
- **Exogeoconservation:** The need to protect geological features of scientific or cultural value.

## 3. NEPA and Potential Sources of Reticence
The US National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is currently limited to actions with a US federal nexus and does not formally apply to extraterrestrial actions. Direct application of NEPA is not recommended as it can be cumbersome and lacks international authority. Instead, space industries should develop their own structured assessment processes.

## 4. Framework for EEA
An EEA should identify direct, indirect, and cumulative impacts. A proposed simplified framework includes:

### 1.0 Introduction
### 2.0 Purpose and Need
Why is the action being undertaken?

### 3.0 Proposed Action
- **Scope:** Detailed narrative of what is to be built and what equipment will be used.
- **Timing:** Launch dates, construction duration, and return dates.
- **Location:** Coordinates, terrain alteration, and road construction.

### 4.0 Affected Environment
- **4.1 Physical Resources:** 
  - *4.1.1 Geology, Regolith, Seismicity:* Vibration impacts, structural stability of formations.
  - *4.1.2 Atmospheric Composition:* Dust generation and its persistence.
  - *4.1.3 Climate:* Changes to local temperature/climate.
  - *4.1.4 Solar Radiation.*
  - *4.1.5 Water Resources:* Location, state (ice/liquid), and chemistry.
- **4.2 Cultural Resources:** Historic/cultural significance.
- **4.3 Hazardous Materials:** Disposition of wastes and chemicals.

### 5.0 Human Health and Safety
Exposure to radiation, extremes, and industrial accidents.

### 6.0 Cumulative Impacts
Impacts from later-in-time mining or consecutive actions.

### 7.0 Summary
Mitigation actions to reduce or eliminate adverse impacts.

## 5. Final Thoughts
EEAs would create a permanent record of baseline conditions and provide a repository of incremental findings. It is critical that commercial interests, governments, and scientific groups collaborate on these standards to avoid repeating Earth's history of environmental degradation.
papers.keyFindings: The paper identifies a critical regulatory gap in protecting extraterrestrial environments from construction and mining impacts. It proposes a voluntary seven-step 'Extraterrestrial Environmental Assessment' (EEA) framework to manage regolith disturbance, dust generation, and water resource depletion.
papers.findings: Proposed a management and planning framework (EEA) to address the environmental consequences of space development activities such as resource extraction and habitat construction.
papers.result: A structured 7-part outline for environmental assessments covering site selection, regolith impact, atmospheric dust generation, water resource usage, and cumulative mission impacts.

papers.relevanceReason: The paper specifically investigates the use of in-situ meteoritic Fe-Ni alloys for constructing pressurized habitats on the Moon and Mars, providing experimental data on material properties and finite element modeling for structural design.
papers.markdownContent:
# Mechanical properties of meteoritic Fe–Ni alloys for in-situ extraterrestrial structures

## Abstract
A critical requirement for outposts and settlements on the Moon and Mars is the use of in-situ resources to create pressurized, human-rated habitats with low mass, high reliability, and easy processability. This study assesses the capability of binary Fe–Ni alloys - with Ni content of 5–11 wt%, typical of M-type asteroids and iron meteorites. Tensile properties increase linearly with Ni content: yield stress from 260 to 440 MPa and UTS from 340 to 560 MPa. A modeled 400 m³ habitat with 1 bar atmosphere requires Fe-7Ni plates of 10 mm thickness to prevent plastic deformation, confirming the feasibility of using processed meteorites for habitat shells.

## 1. Introduction
Extraterrestrial settlements require pressurized habitats made from materials with high tensile strength and toughness. ISRU is favored due to high Earth-to-orbit transport costs. Sintered regolith is weak in tension; Fe-based alloys are better candidates for pressurized thin shells. Fe–Ni alloys are abundant as meteorites on Moon/Mars surfaces or in asteroids. NASA rovers have already identified multiple metallic meteorites on Mars.

## 2. Experimental Study
Binary Fe-xNi alloys (x = 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 wt%) were arc-melted and studied in as-cast conditions. Tensile testing at 21 °C and compression testing down to -89 °C were conducted.

### Table 1: Experimental tensile data measured at 21 °C
| Alloy | Ni % | Grain size (μm) | Yield stress (MPa) | UTS (MPa) | Strain at Failure (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fe–5Ni | 5.0 | 90 | 260 | 342 | 20 |
| Fe–7Ni | 7.1 | 86 | 369 | 427 | 19 |
| Fe–9Ni | 9.2 | 87 | 383 | 444 | 7 |
| Fe–11Ni| 10.9| 91 | 439 | 561 | 3 |

## 3. Finite Element Modeling
FEA was performed using COMSOL to simulate a half-cylindrical 'Quonset hut' habitat (5m radius, 10m length). For a 101 kPa internal pressure under regolith shielding, a shell thickness of 10 mm using Fe–7Ni is sufficient to remain safely below the yield stress despite stress concentrations at welds.

## 5. Conclusions
Fe–Ni alloys from meteorites are suitable for load-bearing structures. Strength increases with Ni content and decreasing temperature. 12 metric tons of alloy are required for a 20-person habitat, which is achievable with 20–30 harvested meteorites.
papers.keyFindings: Binary Fe-Ni alloys found in meteorites (5-11% Ni) provide sufficient yield strength (260-440 MPa) and toughness for pressurized habitat shells. A 10 mm thickness is sufficient for a 5-meter radius Quonset hut under 1 bar of pressure on the Lunar or Martian surface.
papers.findings: Investigation of the mechanical properties of as-cast meteoritic-analog Fe-Ni alloys for structural ISRU applications and evaluation through finite element analysis for habitat viability.
papers.result: Yield stress for Fe-(5-11)Ni increases from 260 to 440 MPa; Fe-7Ni plates of 10 mm thickness (total mass ~12 MT) can support a 400 m³ pressurized volume on Moon/Mars.

papers.title: Role of Cyber-Physical Testing in Developing Resilient Extraterrestrial Habitats
papers.relevanceReason: The paper focuses on the design and validation of resilient extraterrestrial habitats for the Moon and Mars, specifically addressing structural resilience, environmental hazards, and systems engineering for long-term space architecture.
papers.markdownContent:
# Role of Cyber-Physical Testing in Developing Resilient Extraterrestrial Habitats

**Authors:** Amin Maghareh, Ali Lenjani, Murali Krishnan, Shirley Dyke, and Ilias Bilionis
**Publisher:** Earth and Space 2021 (ASCE)

## Abstract
Extraterrestrial long-term habitat systems require groundbreaking technological advances to overcome extreme demands (temperature fluctuations, cosmic rays, dust, meteoroids). This paper highlights the importance of system resilience and cyber-physical testing—integrating physical testing and computational modeling—to address the challenges of developing safe and resilient habitat systems.

## Environmental Conditions
The study compares physical characteristics of Earth, the Moon, and Mars, identifying key hazards for habitat systems.

### Table 1. Physical comparison of Earth, the Moon, and Mars.
| Property | Earth | Moon | Mars |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mass (kg) | 5.97 x 10^24 | 7.35 x 10^22 | 6.42 x 10^23 |
| Spherical radius (km) | 6378 | 1738 | 3393 |
| Equatorial gravity (m/sec) | 9.80 | 1.62 | 3.71 |
| Temperature extremes (°C) | -89 to 58 | -233 to 123 | -153 to 20 |
| Atmospheric pressure (kPa) | 101 | 3 x 10^-12 | 0.4 to 0.87 |
| Surface magnetic field (G) | 0.31 | <= 2 x 10^-3 | <= 5 x 10^-4 |
| Sidereal rotation (day) | 0.997 | 27.322 | 1.03 |

## Key Concepts
- **Resilience:** Defined by three capacities: absorptive, restorative, and adaptive. The paper argues for moving beyond reliability-based design (passive capacity) to resilience-based design (active/adaptive control).
- **Cyber-Physical Testing:** Also known as hybrid simulation, it partitions systems into computational domains (models) and physical domains (specimens) to examine complex interactions cost-effectively.
- **Control-Theoretic Approach:** Proposes a design framework to maximize system plasticity (ability to prevent loss), system rapidity (restoration speed), and minimize lifecycle cost.

## Conclusion
Resilience is critical for habitat success in extreme environments. The Resilient ExtraTerrestrial Habitats research institute (RETHi) is developing a cyber-physical testing platform to validate control-theoretic approaches and evaluate integrated health management models for future space habitats.
papers.keyFindings: The research establishes that traditional reliability-based design is insufficient for complex, tightly-coupled extraterrestrial habitats due to unpredictable disruptions. It identifies cyber-physical testing (hybrid simulation) as a critical, cost-effective methodology for validating habitat resilience and systemic health management under extreme Lunar and Martian conditions.
papers.findings: Habitat resilience requires a comprehensive approach encompassing absorptive, restorative, and adaptive capacities. The paper findings emphasize that habitat systems must be designed as complex, interconnected cyber-physical systems that can autonomously transition between manned and unmanned modes while managing cascading failures.
papers.result: The study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework for habitat design focusing on system plasticity, rapidity, and lifecycle cost. It provides a structured comparison of environmental hazards (Table 1) and details a cyber-physical architecture (Figure 3) used by RETHi to model dynamic habitat reconfiguration during disruptive scenarios.

papers.title: From Rocks to Walls: a Model-free Reinforcement Learning Approach to Dry Stacking with Irregular Rocks
papers.relevanceReason: The paper explores automated construction using in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) on the Moon and Mars, specifically focusing on the dry stacking of irregular, locally-sourced rocks using reinforcement learning to build planetary infrastructure.
papers.markdownContent:
# From Rocks to Walls: a Model-free Reinforcement Learning Approach to Dry Stacking with Irregular Rocks

**André Menezes, Pedro Vicente, Alexandre Bernardino, Rodrigo Ventura**
*Institute for Systems and Robotics, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Portugal*

## Abstract
In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) is a key aspect for an efficient human exploration of extraterrestrial environments. A cost-effective method for the construction of preliminary structures is dry stacking with locally found unprocessed rocks. This work focus on learning this task from scratch. Former approaches rely on previously acquired models of rocks, which may be hard to obtain in the context of a mission. In alternative, we propose a model-free, data driven approach. We formulate the problem as the task of selecting the position to place each rock on top of the currently built structure. The rocks are presented to the robot in sequence. The goal is to assemble a wall that approximates a target volume, given the 3D perception of the currently built structure, the next object and the target volume. An agent is developed to learn this task using reinforcement learning. The deep Q-networks (DQN) algorithm is used, where the Q-network outputs a value map corresponding to the expected return of placing the object in each position of a top-view depth image. The learned policy outperforms engineered heuristics, both in terms of stability of the structure and similarity with the target volume. Despite the simplification of the task, the policy learned with this approach could be applied to a realistic setting as the high level planner in an autonomous construction pipeline.

## 1. Introduction
For a long term human exploration of extraterrestrial environments, such as the Moon and Mars, it is essential to use native materials as replacement to resources otherwise brought from Earth at great expense. This is commonly referred to as in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) and, amongst other applications, is useful for the construction of planetary infrastructures [13]. Initial settlement structures, such as roads, platforms and shade walls, may be built with unprocessed or minimally processed local rocks using the ancient method of dry stacking [16]. Although rudimentary, this technique has been proven to produce long lasting structures, while requiring very low pre-processing time and energy. Due to the increased risk and limitations imposed by human missions [1], it is important to have systems with the capability of autonomously setting up infrastructure.

However, assembling a structure from a set of irregularly shaped rocks is a difficult task, usually performed by experienced humans and requiring some amount of intuition. It is not clear how to translate this into an autonomous system, specially in a country where no models of the environment are available. Model-based approaches are not suitable within this context. For this reason, the problem of dry stacking in extra-terrestrial environments requires a learning from scratch and model-free approach.

## 4. Results
A set of experiments is performed on the described environment, simulated using PyBullet. The dataset of rock models used is composed of 500 models generated with each value of irregularity, resulting in a complete dataset of 5500 models. The size of the overhead and object elevation maps are 128 x 128 and 32 x 32, respectively. The episode length t is set to 30 objects. Two metrics are used to evaluate the obtained policies. The first is the IoU, which is a measurement of the similarity between the built and target volumes. The second is the average of the discounts (AD), which evaluates the effectiveness and stability of the placements.

| Method | IoU_30 | AD_30 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Learned with IoU | 0.266 (0.026) | 0.584 (0.064) |
| Learned with DIoU | 0.303 (0.029) | 0.791 (0.058) |
| Random | 0.125 (0.027) | 0.738 (0.060) |
| Random (goal) | 0.232 (0.025) | 0.507 (0.064) |
| Cross-correlation | 0.27 (0.024) | 0.769 (0.046) |

## 5. Conclusion and Future Works
The major achievement of this work was to develop a setup in which a dry stacking policy can be learned without any previously acquired models of the environment. An agent is able to learn from scratch a policy that captures the goal of the environment and its dynamics. The emerged behavior is, to some extent, consistent with dry stacking theory [20]. The agent learned the policy using a model-free approach in simulation, which can be directly used in extra-terrestrial environments since the agent is not based on pre-existent models. Our data-driven approach is more suitable for ISRU.
papers.keyFindings: The research successfully demonstrates a model-free reinforcement learning framework for the autonomous assembly of dry-stacked rock walls using local irregular materials. A novel reward metric called Discounted Intersection over Union (DIoU) was found to significantly enhance structural stability and alignment with target designs compared to standard metrics and heuristics.
papers.findings: The study identifies that model-free Deep Q-Networks (DQN) can effectively manage the complex task of stacking irregular rocks for ISRU construction without requiring pre-scanned geometric models of the rocks. It highlights that incorporating stability constraints directly into the reward function via spatial discounting leads to more robust wall construction suitable for planetary environments.
papers.result: The 'Learned with DIoU' model outperformed all others, achieving a terminal Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.303 and a structural stability (Average Discount) of 0.791, surpassing the engineered cross-correlation heuristic (IoU 0.27, AD 0.769).

papers.title: Determining the yield stress of a Biopolymer-bound Soil Composite for extrusion-based 3D printing applications
papers.relevanceReason: The paper focuses on the development of Biopolymer-bound Soil Composites (BSC) using lunar regolith simulant for extrusion-based 3D printing, which is a direct application of ISRU and automated construction for space habitats.
papers.keyFindings: Biopolymer-bound Soil Composites (BSC) using lunar regolith simulant and blood protein are viable for 3D printing within a specific soil volume fraction range (0.435–0.548). The research establishes that thixotropy in these materials is primarily caused by particle reconsolidation rather than chemical bonding, with a regime transition from hydrodynamic to frictional behavior occurring at ϕ_{BSC} = 0.52. The study provides predictive mathematical models for static and dynamic yield stress to ensure material pumpability and structural shape stability in lunar construction scenarios.
papers.findings: The researchers developed and validated two rheological models: a hydrodynamic model (Chateau-Ovarlez-Trung) and a frictional model (De Larrard). They identified that the transition from a hydrodynamic-dominated regime to a frictional-dominated regime occurs at a soil volume fraction of 0.52.
papers.result: A printable soil volume fraction range for lunar regolith BSC was determined to be 0.435 to 0.548. Static yield stress values for the tested mixtures ranged from 46 Pa to 3644 Pa. Extrusion was limited to mixtures where the soil volume fraction was less than 80% of the maximum packing fraction (ϕ_{mp} = 0.689 for JSC-1A).

papers.relevanceReason: The paper investigates microbially-enhanced mining (biomining) of vanadium from basalt, an abundant material on the Moon and Mars, for use in high-strength structural materials. This is directly relevant to ISRU and space habitat construction strategies.
papers.markdownContent:
# Microbially-Enhanced Vanadium Mining and Bioremediation Under Micro- and Mars Gravity on the International Space Station

**Authors:** Charles S. Cockell, Rosa Santomartino, Kai Finster, Annemiek C. Waajen, Natasha Nicholson, Claire-Marie Loudon, Lorna J. Eades, Ralf Moeller, Petra Rettberg, Felix M. Fuchs, Rob Van Houdt, Natalie Leys, Ilse Coninx, Jason Hatton, Luca Parmitano, Jutta Krause, Andrea Koehler, Nicol Caplin, Lobke Zuijderduijn, Alessandro Mariani, Stefano Pellari, Fabrizio Carubia, Giacomo Luciani, Michele Balsamo, Valfredo Zolesi, Jon Ochoa, Pia Sen, James A. J. Watt, Jeannine Doswald-Winkler, Magdalena Herová, Bernd Rattenbacher, Jennifer Wadsworth, R. Craig Everroad and René Demets

**Published:** 01 April 2021  
**Journal:** Frontiers in Microbiology  
**DOI:** 10.3389/fmicb.2021.641387

## Abstract
As humans explore and settle in space, they will need to mine elements to support industries such as manufacturing and construction. In preparation for the establishment of permanent human settlements across the Solar System, we conducted the ESA BioRock experiment on board the International Space Station to investigate whether biological mining could be accomplished under extraterrestrial gravity conditions. We tested the hypothesis that the gravity (g) level influenced the efficacy with which biomining could be achieved from basalt, an abundant material on the Moon and Mars, by quantifying bioleaching by three different microorganisms under microgravity, simulated Mars and Earth gravitational conditions. 

## Key Findings
- *Sphingomonas desiccabilis* and *Bacillus subtilis* significantly enhanced vanadium leaching from basalt compared to sterile controls.
- Gravity conditions (microgravity, simulated Mars, and Earth gravity) did not significantly influence the mean leaching efficacy.
- Bioleaching can achieve an approximate two-fold increase in vanadium leaching over non-biological processes in space environments.

## Methods
- **Microorganisms:** *Sphingomonas desiccabilis* CP1D, *Bacillus subtilis* NCIB 3610, and *Cupriavidus metallidurans* CH34.
- **Substrate:** Olivine basalt rock collected from Iceland (Moon/Mars analog).
- **Hardware:** ESA BioRock apparatus containing Experiment Units (EU) with culture medium reservoirs and gas-permeable membranes.
- **Experiment Duration:** 21 days on the International Space Station (ISS).

## Results

### Table 1: Data associated with the biomining of vanadium
| Organism | Condition | Quantity (ng) | Comparison with control (%) | Comparison with quantity in basalt (%) x 10^-4 | Percentage leached in cell pellet (%) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| | Mars gravity | 23.45 ± 2.70 | 216.32 ± 68.43 | 71.65 ± 8.25 | 1.69 ± 0.40 |

| *B. subtilis* | Microgravity | 30.38 ± 3.90 | 283.22 ± 116.44 | 92.82 ± 11.91 | 0.96 ± 0.36 |

| Sterile ISS control| Microgravity | 10.73 ± 4.19 | - | 32.77 ± 12.80 | - |
| | Mars gravity | 10.84 ± 3.19 | - | 33.12 ± 9.76 | - |
| | Earth gravity | 10.30 ± 2.65 | - | 31.47 ± 8.09 | - |

## Conclusion
The results demonstrate the potential for biological vanadium sequestration under Martian and asteroidal gravity conditions. This demonstrates that microbial cellular metabolism remains functional in diverse gravity environments, enabling the use of bioreactors for ISRU, bioremediation, and recycling to support long-term human presence and extraterrestrial construction.
papers.keyFindings: The research confirms that biomining of vanadium from basalt is feasible under microgravity and simulated Mars gravity, with *Sphingomonas desiccabilis* and *Bacillus subtilis* increasing leaching efficacy by up to 283% compared to sterile controls. Crucially, the study found that gravity levels did not significantly impact the bioleaching results, supporting the use of biological ISRU processes across various planetary bodies.
papers.findings: The study validates that heterotrophic microorganisms can successfully extract metals from volcanic rocks in space. It establishes that altered gravity (micro- and Mars-g) does not inhibit the bioleaching process for vanadium, providing a proof-of-concept for biological ISRU in space settlement scenarios.
papers.result: Vanadium leaching was enhanced by 184.92% to 283.22% across gravity conditions using *S. desiccabilis* and *B. subtilis*. In contrast, *C. metallidurans* did not show significant enhancement. Final quantities of vanadium leached into the medium ranged from approximately 20 to 30 ng per sample in the biological setups compared to ~10 ng in sterile controls.

papers.title: Numerical Simulation of 3D Printing of Infrastructure Materials
papers.relevanceReason: The paper focuses on the numerical simulation of 3D printing for infrastructure, specifically applying the model to the construction of a Martian habitat using ISRU-based additive manufacturing techniques.
papers.markdownContent:
# Numerical Simulation of 3D Printing of Infrastructure Materials

**Authors:** E. Ramyar, Z. Xinwei, G. Cusatis
**Published in:** Earth and Space 2021 (ASCE)

## Abstract
3D printing is a disruptive force for terrestrial and extraterrestrial infrastructure development. This paper highlights the formulation of the Discrete Fresh Concrete Model (DFCM), a particle-based cementitious material model that simulates rheological and mechanical behavior during and after printing. The model uses visco-plastic constitutive equations based on stress-strain relationships to allow a seamless transition from fresh to hardened concrete states.

## Introduction
Concrete 3D printing requires adapting technologies to the rheological characteristics of concrete and developing new materials. Computational models are essential for the design and optimization of printed structures, particularly for autonomous remote operations in extraterrestrial environments like Mars.

## Discrete Fresh Concrete Model (DFCM)
DFCM adopts rigid composite spherical particles to simulate coarse aggregate surrounded by soft mortar (the "excess paste theory").
- **Mechanics:** Contact behavior is governed by a combination of parallel and series nonlinear springs and viscous dashpots.
- **Constitutive Equations:** Formulated in terms of stress-strain relationships (unlike conventional force-displacement models), facilitating the use of parameters identical to those used for hardened concrete.
- **Key Parameters:** Tensile strength, mortar normal modulus, shear yield stress, plastic viscosity, and mortar thickness.

## Experimental Validation
The model was validated against two standard tests:
1.  **Slump Test:** Successfully simulated Self-Consolidating Concrete (SCC) spread (60 cm diameter/25 cm slump) and printable concrete (minimal slump of a few centimeters).
2.  **ICAR Rheometer Test:** Matched experimental torque-speed data for both regular and printable concrete mixes.

## Application: Northwestern Martian Habitat
In collaboration with Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM), Northwestern University designed a dome-shaped Martian habitat for NASA’s 3D-Printed Habitat Challenge. The DFCM was used to simulate the layer-by-layer printing process, accounting for:
- Nozzle-particle and inter-particle rheological interactions.
- Material discharge rates dependent on gravity and pump pressure.
- Autonomous construction monitoring and optimization.

## Conclusion
The DFCM accurately simulates the rheological behavior of cementitious materials for 3D printing. The model's successful replication of experimental ICAR and slump tests demonstrates its reliability for simulating construction processes on other planets.
papers.keyFindings: The research introduces the Discrete Fresh Concrete Model (DFCM) which uses stress-strain based constitutive equations to accurately simulate the rheology and placement of 3D-printed concrete. The model successfully validated terrestrial material tests and was used to simulate the autonomous, layer-by-layer construction of a Martian dome habitat.
papers.findings: The DFCM provides a robust framework for simulating the transition of concrete from a fresh, flowable state to a hardened state using a single set of constitutive equations. It identifies that printable concrete for space applications is significantly less rate-dependent than standard concrete, requiring high shear yield stress and low plastic viscosity.
papers.result: The model accurately matched experimental torque resistant values for printable concrete in rheometer tests and simulated the 3D-printing sequence of the Northwestern Martian Habitat, confirming the compatibility of nozzle velocity with material discharge rates under specific gravity conditions.

papers.title: Optimizing Magnesium Phosphate Binders with Boric Acid for Additive Construction Applications
papers.relevanceReason: The paper discusses the use of magnesium phosphate cement (MPC) as an ISRU-based material for 3D construction of extraterrestrial habitats on the Moon and Mars.
papers.markdownContent:
# Optimizing Magnesium Phosphate Binders with Boric Acid for Additive Construction Applications

**Authors:** H. Alkhateb; H. Almashaqbeh; J. Edmunson; M. Fiske; Y. Najjar; and Damian Stoddard  
**Publication:** Earth and Space 2021, ASCE

## Abstract
The authors propose a framework to utilize magnesia-based binders (MBBs) as an ordinary portland cement (OPC) alternative for extraterrestrial habitats. MBBs show promise for additive construction (AC) due to high compressive strength, rapid setting, and potential for harvesting from lunar and Martian regolith. The research focuses on magnesia phosphate cement (MPC) with boric acid additives to optimize setting time for 3D printing. Artificial neural networks (ANN) are used to investigate and optimize formulations.

## Introduction
Additive Manufacturing (AM) in construction reduces costs and time, but planetary autonomous construction faces challenges regarding printable materials in extreme environments. Utilizing in-situ resources (ISRU) for habitat structures on the Moon and Mars reduces Earth-launched payloads. MPC, formed by reacting magnesium oxide with phosphate compounds, is a candidate binder as Moon/Mars surfaces are rich in magnesium-bearing minerals. However, MPC's extremely rapid setting time (seconds) must be controlled for AC.

## Magnesium Phosphate Cements
MPC belongs to the chemically bonded ceramics (CBCs) group. The main reaction produces K-struvite (MgKPO4·6H2O). The study explores factors tailoring MPC properties: M/P (magnesia to phosphate) molar ratio, W/S (water to solid) ratio, and retarders like boric acid (H3BO3).

## Methodology
The experimental program studied the effect of boric acid on MPC performance using M/P, W/P, and B/M (boric acid to magnesia) ratios. ANN models were developed to predict performance.

### Materials
- **MgO:** Dead-burned magnesium oxide (98% purity).
- **Phosphate:** Monopotassium phosphate (KDP).
- **Retarder:** Boric acid (99.9% purity).

### Table 1: Chemical composition of dead-burned MgO powder
| Magnesium Oxide (MgO)% | Silicon Oxide (SiO2)% | Calcium Oxide (CaO)% | Iron Oxide (Fe2O3)% | Aluminum Oxide (Al2O3)% |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 98.00 | 0.70 | 0.95 | 0.15 | 0.20 |

### Table 2: Physical and chemical properties of boric acid powder
| Physical/chemical property | Description/Measured value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Appearance | Crystalline, White Solid |
| pH | 5.1 at 1.8 g/l at 25 °C |
| Melting point | 160 °C |
| Initial boiling point | 1860 °C |
| Relative density | 1.440 g/cm3 |
| Solubility | In Water: 4.7% @ 20°C |
| Decomposition temp | 169±1 to HBO2 |

## Results and Discussion
- **Influence of Boric Acid:** Increasing B/M ratio up to 5% increases initial setting time. Beyond 5%, setting time may decrease due to fluidity loss. Boric acid forms a temporary lunebergite layer that hinders cation dissolution.
- **Mechanical Properties:** For low M/P ratios, boric acid significantly reduces compressive strength (up to 64% reduction at 10% B/M). For high M/P ratios, the effect is marginal.
- **ANN Simulation:** A 5-5-3 feed-forward backpropagation model successfully predicted MPC properties (flow, setting time, strength) with an R2 of 0.89.

## Conclusions
MPC fresh and hardened properties can be tailored for 3D printing by manipulating M/P, W/P, and B/M ratios. Using up to 5% boric acid improves setting time for construction, but excessive amounts impact strength. Molar ratio representation provides better understanding than weight ratios for MPC behavior.
papers.keyFindings: Boric acid effectively retards the rapid setting of magnesium phosphate cement, extending the initial setting window to 15 minutes, which is necessary for additive construction. The study establishes that molar ratios (M/P and W/P) are superior to weight ratios for optimizing in-situ construction materials for Moon and Mars environments.
papers.findings: The study investigates magnesia phosphate cement (MPC) as an ISRU binder for planetary habitats, specifically focusing on the use of boric acid as a retarder to facilitate additive manufacturing. It highlights that the optimal mix depends on the interaction between magnesia-to-phosphate ratios and water content, which can be accurately modeled using artificial neural networks.
papers.result: Initial setting time was increased from 3.5 to 15 minutes by adding 5% boric acid to a specific MPC mix (M/P 3, W/P 2.2). Compressive strengths peaked at approximately 55 MPa for an M/P ratio of 6, while an ANN model achieved a training R2 of 0.93 and a validation R2 of 0.77 for predicting material performance.

papers.title: Applying Terrestrial Geo-Material Science Methodology to Lunar ISRU Construction
papers.relevanceReason: The paper specifically addresses the characterization of lunar regolith and the evaluation of ISRU construction methods including sintering, concreting (geopolymers/sulfur), and additive manufacturing for lunar infrastructure.
papers.markdownContent:
# Applying Terrestrial Geo-Material Science Methodology to Lunar ISRU Construction

**Authors:** H. Patel, P. Suermann, N. Shumaker, S. Deitrick, J. W. Bullard, and R. C. Ewing

**Published in:** Earth and Space 2021

## Abstract
Building on research for military and expeditionary construction, this research aims to establish methods for the design and testing of material mixtures derived from the lunar surface with minimal additives. The paper reviews opportunities and challenges of methods like concreting and sintering and discusses the need for highland-specific regolith simulants for the Artemis missions.

## Introduction
There is a pressing need for construction methods using in-situ materials for critical lunar infrastructure like landing pads, roads, and radiation shielding. The lack of in-situ geotechnical site assessment on the Moon necessitates predictive methodologies for geotechnical properties.

## Background: Lunar surface environment
*   **Mare Regions:** ~15% of surface, basaltic, relatively young, thinner regolith.
*   **Highlands:** Anorthositic, much older, thicker regolith, higher agglutinate content.
*   **Regolith Properties:** Fine-grained (avg 72 μm), bulk density 1.30 to 1.92 g/cm³. 95% of mass <1.37 mm.

### Agglutinates
Fused particles of impact glass and mineral fragments. Content ranges from 5% to 65% by volume. They introduce unique chemical and physical properties that affect construction material performance.

## Construction Methods and Considerations
1.  **Concreting:** Binding grains in a matrix. Challenges include scarcity of water and calcium on the Moon. Alternatives include geopolymers (aluminosilicate precursors) and sulfur binders (melting point ~115°C).
2.  **Sintering:** Fusing grains via heat. Lunar regolith mineral constituents (aluminosilicates) have relatively low melting temperatures (800°C to 1000°C). Challenges include the coarse particle size (70 μm) compared to industrial sintering powders.
3.  **Additive Construction:** Can be extrusion-based (concreting) or powder-bed based (sintering).

## Methodology: THAMES
The Thermodynamic Hydration and Microstructure Evolution Simulator (THAMES) is used to predict mineralogical components and simulate 3D virtual microstructures to calculate engineering properties of binders.

## Conclusion
The research aims to identify how existing terrestrial models can be adapted to evaluate regolith-based materials under lunar conditions, eventually leading to ASCE/ASTM standards for ISRU construction.
papers.keyFindings: The research identifies that while sintering and concreting are primary candidates for lunar construction, obstacles such as the coarse particle size of lunar regolith and the scarcity of water must be overcome. The study proposes the use of thermodynamic modeling (THAMES) and the development of highlands-specific simulants with realistic agglutinate content to accurately predict material performance.
papers.findings: The paper outlines a methodology for lunar ISRU construction by adapting terrestrial geo-material science. It emphasizes the distinct differences between lunar mare and highland regolith, particularly the higher agglutinate content in the latter. It identifies Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) and sulfur-based or geopolymer-based concreting as high-potential technologies for lunar infrastructure.
papers.result: Lunar regolith has an average particle size of 72 μm and bulk density of 1.30-1.92 g/cm³. Sulfur, present at ~1% mass in regolith, melts at 115°C. Regolith mineral constituents have melting temperatures between 800°C and 1000°C. Agglutinate content in older lunar surfaces ranges from 5% to 65% by volume.

papers.title: Energy Life Cycle in Extraterrestrial Construction Projects: Is Building Underground an Option?
papers.relevanceReason: The paper investigates the energy feasibility of underground construction on Mars, specifically analyzing the energy required for regolith excavation and soil removal, which is critical for Class III (ISRU-based) space habitat construction.
papers.markdownContent:
# Energy Life Cycle in Extraterrestrial Construction Projects: Is Building Underground an Option?

**Authors:** Hashem Izadi Moud, Peyman Rahgozar, Sebastian T. Weber, Craig Capano, and Ian Flood
**Conference:** Earth and Space 2021
**Publisher:** ASCE

## ABSTRACT
Making life multi-planetary requires substantial knowledge of building structures in extraterrestrial bodies, where natural resources are scarce, human resources are expensive-to-utilize, and energy sources are vastly different from the Earth. Solar energy is expected to be the primary source for extraterrestrial construction projects. This paper presents energy cycle flowcharts for construction projects on Earth and beyond and argues about the expensive and unrealistic nature of building underground due to high energy consumption.

## INTRODUCTION
Future shelters must protect occupants from extreme conditions including lack of atmosphere, meteorite impacts, lack of magnetic fields, and radiation. Colonization is proposed as a three-phase program: (1) short-term missions, (2) slightly longer stays, and (3) permanent colonization. While modular structures can be shipped from Earth, the cost of transportation makes large-scale colonization dependent on ISRU and local energy sources.

## ENERGY IN CONSTRUCTION
### On Earth
Construction Management (CM) focuses on the "iron triangle": time, cost, and scope. Energy is rarely a priority due to the abundance of cheap fossil fuels. This access allows for massive infrastructure like underground subways and skyscrapers.

### In Space
Multiplanetary life requires a reliable energy source. Transportation of fossil fuels from Earth is cost-prohibitive ($15,000 - $45,000 per kg). Solar energy is the most common form available but faces challenges such as low intensity and long nights on Mars.

## CASE STUDY: BUILDING UNDERGROUND ON MARS
The study estimates the energy needed to build a small underground room requiring 600 cubic meters (m³) of space. Accounting for soil stability, ramps for machinery, and backfill, the total volume of soil to be removed is calculated at 1800 m³.

### Technical Calculations
- **Excavation Energy (Earth base):** 12.09 MJ/m³ for Silty Sand.
- **Total Energy for 1800 m³:** 21,762 MJ or 6,045 kWh.
- **Solar Radiance on Mars:** Yearly mean is ~200 W/m².
- **Solar Panel Efficiency:** Assumed at 30%.
- **Harvesting Capacity:** ~655.20 Wh/m²/day.

### Results
Using a 400 m² solar field (yielding 264 kWh per Martian day), it would take approximately **29 Martian Days (Sols)** just to harvest the energy required for excavation of a single 600 m³ room.

## DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
Underground construction using large-scale equipment like Tunnel Boring Machines (TBM) is energy-intensive. Without fossil fuels, developing cities beyond Earth requires a combination of:
1. Ultra-efficient and sustainable design of structures.
2. Smart and resource-efficient planning.
3. Energy-efficient construction techniques and machinery.

Building underground might not be a feasible option for initial large-scale colonization due to these extreme energy constraints.
papers.keyFindings: Excavating 1800 m³ of soil for a small 600 m³ underground room on Mars requires approximately 6045 kWh of energy. Harvesting this energy with a 400 m² solar field would take nearly 29 Martian days, suggesting that extensive excavation-based construction is currently impractical compared to other methods.
papers.findings: The study highlights the fundamental shift from the fossil-fuel-driven construction cycle on Earth to a solar-energy-constrained cycle in space. It concludes that building underground is economically and energetically unfeasible for early permanent colonization due to the massive energy requirements of soil removal and the low energy density of solar harvesting compared to Earth's energy infrastructure.
papers.result: Total soil removal for a 600 m³ room equals 1800 m³; total energy for excavation is 6045 kWh; solar harvesting capacity on Mars is ~655.20 Wh/m²/day with 30% efficient panels.

papers.title: Designing Biopolymer-Bound Regolith Composites for Maximum Compressive Strength
papers.relevanceReason: The paper investigates the development of biopolymer-bound soil composites (BSC) using lunar regolith simulant (JSC-1A) for extraterrestrial construction, focusing on ISRU materials and structural performance.
papers.markdownContent:
# Designing Biopolymer-Bound Regolith Composites for Maximum Compressive Strength

**Authors:** I. Rosa, A. Coto, M. I. Allende, M. D. Lepech, and D. J. Loftus
**Affiliations:** Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Stanford Univ.; Space Bioscience Research Division, NASA Ames Research Center.
**Conference:** Earth and Space 2021 (ASCE)

## Abstract
Extraterrestrial construction presents challenges due to the cost of transporting materials from Earth. This work focuses on a novel class of biopolymer-bound soil composite (BSC) materials produced by desiccating a mixture of soil, water, and a biopolymer binder (bovine blood plasma proteins). Nineteen BSC mixes using JSC-1A regolith were tested. A maximum compressive strength of 25 MPa was obtained. A design tool is introduced for future structural design on the Moon, Mars, or other bodies.

## 1. Introduction
The study addresses the need for sustainable construction materials that use local resources and low energy. BSC materials leverage natural binders and locally sourced aggregates to create a circular material system suitable for long-duration space missions.

## 2. Experimental Design
The study translates BSC design methodology to lunar regolith using JSC-1A simulant. Key parameters include soil maximum bulk density, biopolymer solution concentration, and biopolymer solution density. Dried bovine blood plasma proteins (BSA and immunoglobins) were used as the binder.

## 3. Materials and Experimental Methods
- **Inorganic Aggregate:** JSC-1A simulant.
- **Binder:** AP920 Bovine Plasma.
- **Manufacturing:** Dry-mixing of aggregate and protein, adding water, blending, and compacting at 5 MPa in a cylindrical mold (2:1 height-to-diameter ratio). Specimens were desiccated at 60°C for 24 hours.
- **Testing:** Unconfined uniaxial compression testing using an MTS Criterion Model 43.

## 4. Experimental Results
Results show compressive strength and density for various mixes (Table 2). A maximum strength of 25.4 MPa was achieved with the BPS-48_BS-12 mix.

### Table 2: JSC-1A/AP920 Material Characteristics and Mechanical Properties (Selection)
| Mix Name | Biopolymer Conc. | Biopolymer Soil Ratio | Dry Density (g/cm³) | Compressive Strength (MPa) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| BPS-30_BS-04 | 29% | 4% | 1.74 | 7.3 |
| BPS-38_BS-10 | 38% | 10% | 1.89 | 17.6 |
| BPS-43_BS-10 | 43% | 10% | 1.91 | 20.6 |
| BPS-48_BS-12 | 48% | 12% | 1.97 | 25.4 |
| BPS-53_BS-13 | 52% | 13% | 1.89 | 18.6 |

## 5. Models for Predicting Bulk Density and Compressive Strength
Linear and mixed-effects models were developed to predict dry bulk density and compressive strength as functions of biopolymer concentration and soil ratio. The linear model for compressive strength showed an R-squared value of 0.967.

## 6. Discussion
Saturation ratios above unity (oversaturation) result in decreased compressive strength due to shrinkage-induced damage in the biopolymer matrix. Strength follows a linear relationship with bulk density and biopolymer-to-soil ratio when the saturation ratio is ≤ 1.0.

## 7. Conclusions & Future Work
BSC materials exhibited a linear relationship between strength and density/binder ratio. Future work will explore 3D printing and alternate manufacturing methods to achieve higher bulk densities closer to dry compaction levels.
papers.keyFindings: Biopolymer-bound soil composites (BSC) using lunar simulant can reach compressive strengths of 25 MPa, meeting concrete standards. The material performance is optimized when the biopolymer solution saturation ratio is maintained below unity to prevent shrinkage damage.
papers.findings: The research confirms that BSC design theory originally developed for sand is applicable to lunar regolith simulant. It identifies that the maximum bulk density and compressive strength are highly dependent on the biopolymer solution concentration and the saturation ratio of the mixture.
papers.result: A maximum compressive strength of 25.4 MPa was achieved at a biopolymer concentration of 48% and a biopolymer-to-soil ratio of 12.3% (Mix BPS-48_BS-12).

papers.relevanceReason: While the study focuses on terrestrial residential housing, the methodology regarding BIM-based generative design, automated planning for prefabricated components, and waste optimization algorithms is directly applicable to the systems engineering and automated construction planning required for space habitat Class I and Class II structures.
