# Building Information Modelling- (BIM-) Based Generative Design for Drywall Installation Planning in Prefabricated Construction

**Authors:** Jose Daniel Cuellar Lobo, Zhen Lei, Hexu Liu, Hong Xian Li, and SangHyeok Han

**Publication:** Advances in Civil Engineering, Volume 2021, Article ID 6638236

**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/6638236

## Abstract
In prefabricated construction, building components are manufactured off-site before shipping to the site for installation. This study proposes a generative design approach that utilizes the optimization of the drywall installation layout to improve overall project efficiency. The framework includes a decision support module that considers environmental, cost, and aesthetic aspects to identify the optimal layout. The framework's practical applicability has been successfully demonstrated through a case study.

## 1. Introduction
Prefabrication takes a manufacturing style to produce building components off-site and ship them to the installation site. In the North American housing industry, residential houses are often constructed using wood products. Gypsum and plywood sheathing materials come in standard sizes, and their installation often involves cutting material into smaller pieces, generating scrap waste. Prefabricated construction provides opportunities to improve the sheathing installation practice through controlled environments and BIM-based optimization.

## 2. Methodology
The research methodology consists of four analytical modules and one visualization module:
1.  **Data Extraction:** Geometrical information (wall frame coordinates) and material properties are extracted from the BIM 3D model (Revit).
2.  **Simulation-Based Design Algorithm:** Uses parameterized inputs to generate multiple feasible layout alternatives.
3.  **Heuristic Optimization Algorithm:** A greedy algorithm is used to locally optimize material waste for each design alternative by reusing cuts.
4.  **Decision-Making Support:** A fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) methodology is implemented to rank design alternatives based on environmental, cost, and aesthetic criteria.
5.  **Visualization:** Results are returned to Dynamo for visualization in the BIM environment.

### Table 1: Sample cost information for drywall material and productivity (Canadian market)
| Item | Cost/Price | Units | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Drywall (4x8 ft) | $13 | $CAD/unit | Home Depot |
| Installation | $50 | $CAD/hr | Industry partner |
| Finishing | $70 | $CAD/hr | Industry partner |
| Landfill fee | $28 | $CAD/tonne | Fundy Recycles |

## 3. Implementation and Case Study
A two-story wood residential house (53 wood frames) was used as a case study. Thirty simulation cycles were initiated to generate drywall layouts based on different sizes (4x8, 4x10). Design rules included vertical/horizontal orientation checks, staggering seams (1/8 in. gap), and avoiding joints at high-stress areas like door/window openings.

## 4. Results and Discussion
The study achieved the following improvements compared to the simulation median:
*   **Environmental:** 37.5% reduction in material waste (achieving a 10% minimum waste percentage).
*   **Cost:** 7% reduction in total project cost (CAD 5,580 median vs optimized).
*   **Aesthetic:** 54% reduction in drywall seam length (231 lin. ft. median vs optimized).

### Table 6: Final fuzzy AHP scores (Top 5 scenarios)
| Top 10 | Scenario | Aesthetic | Environmental | Total Cost | Final Fuzzy AHP Score |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | s25 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2.66 |
| 2 | s65 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2.66 |
| 3 | s62 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2.34 |
| 4 | s88 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2.34 |
| 5 | s117 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2.34 |

## 5. Conclusions
The framework provides a systematic way to explore multiple design alternatives. The research demonstrated that the "best" design layout is conditional on the prioritization of management criteria (e.g., waste vs. aesthetics). The contributions include generative design for prefabrication planning and the integration of fuzzy AHP for results evaluation.
papers.keyFindings: The study develops a BIM-integrated generative design framework that optimizes the layout of prefabricated components to minimize waste and cost while maximizing aesthetic quality. Using a fuzzy AHP decision-support model, the researchers achieved up to 37.5% waste reduction and 7% cost savings in a prefabricated wood-frame construction case study.
papers.findings: Development of a four-stage analytical framework for automated construction design: data extraction, simulation-based layout generation, greedy heuristic optimization for material reuse, and fuzzy AHP multicriteria decision analysis.
papers.result: The implemented framework achieved a minimum material waste of 10% (37.5% reduction from median) and a 54% reduction in seam length compared to standard planning practices for a 53-frame residential structure.

# A new deployable pantographic lunar habitat

**Authors:** Amin Lak, Maziar Asefi
**Journal:** Acta Astronautica 192 (2022) 351–367
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.actaastro.2021.12.049

## Abstract
Deployable lunar structures address the volumetric limitations of cargo flights. This paper introduces a habitat using linear and planar elements connected via movable joints, utilizing modified polar and angulated scissor-like elements (SLE). An experimental study assessed deployment strategies and dimensional properties for a four-person crew.

## 1. Introduction
Habitat design approaches range from rigid hard-shell modules (Class I) to deployable units (Class II) and ISRU-based structures (Class III). Deployable structures are preferred due to low packaging volume.

## 2. Design Considerations
Key hazards include micrometeoroids, radiation, and vacuum. Design criteria emphasize simple mechanical connections, modularity, and common components for ease of maintenance and replacement.

### Table 1: Different types of class-II structures
| Type | Strategy applied within |
| :--- | :--- |
| Inflatable | Multi-layered membrane inflated after landing. |
| Erectable | Set of rigid elements assembled on-site. |
| Hybrid | Inflatable membrane combined with rigid elements or ISRU. |

## 3. Concepts Assessment
The study evaluates three existing concepts: Trigon, Inflated-torus, and Moon Base Two.

### Table 3: Assessment results (Summary)
| Criterion | TRIGON | Inflated-torus | Moon-base two |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Volume expansion ratio | 6 | 4 | 6 |
| Pre-launch integration | 3 | 5 | 5 |
| Protection | 5 | 4 | 6 |
| Ease of Assembly | 1 | 5 | 1 |
| Automation | 2 | 6 | 1 |
| **Sum** | **17 points** | **24 points** | **19 points** |

## 4. Scissor-hinge systems
Planar scissor structural mechanisms (SSM) are formed by connecting scissor units (SU). Types include translational, polar, and angulated units defined by the pivot point and bar geometry.

## 5. Design

### 5.1 Habitat Dimensions
Based on NASA standards, a minimum net habitable volume (NHV) of 25 m³/crewmember is recommended. For a 180-day mission, 40 m³/crewmember is suggested, leading to a total needed floor area of 45.6 m² for four people.

### 5.3 Mechanism Design
The proposed structure uses:
- Two identical loops of angulated SLE units.
- A central structural core.
- Modified polar SLE (MP-SLE) units for the roof.
- Rigid panels for shielding and flooring.

### Table 4: Angulated element and loop properties
| Property | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Bar length | 0.65 m |
| Kink angle | 18° |
| Number of units | 20 |
| Deployed radius | 3.80 m |
| Maximum area | 45.40 m² |

### 5.3.9 Material selection
- **Shielding:** Carbon composite for rigid panels.
- **Membrane:** Multi-layer including Vectran or Kevlar restraint layers, redundant pressure bladders, and MLI thermal protection.

### 5.3.10 Actuating mechanism
Deployment is driven by a central telescopic jack that slides the movable intermediate connection elements (MICE) along the z-axis.

## 6. Conclusions
The design provides a nominal internal volume of ~170 m³ for a 180-day mission. The hybrid approach combines the quick deployment of inflatable structures with the protection of rigid systems.

### Table 8: Habitat overall properties
| Prototype geometry | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Maximum internal height | 4.42 m |
| Nominal floor area | 45.40 m² |
| Nominal interior volume | 169.2 m³ |
papers.keyFindings: The study develops a hybrid deployable lunar habitat using pantographic scissor-like elements that achieve an internal volume of 169.2 m³ from a compact launch configuration. The design effectively balances the rapid deployment characteristic of inflatables with the structural protection provided by rigid carbon-composite shielding panels.
papers.findings: The research concludes that a hybrid structural system using modified polar and angulated scissor-like elements provides superior pre-launch integration and deployment automation compared to purely inflatable or erectable systems. It identifies specific geometric configurations and material stacks (including Kevlar and carbon composites) that optimize the habitat for a four-person crew on a 180-day lunar mission.
papers.result: The resulting habitat design offers a floor area of 45.40 m², a maximum internal height of 4.42 m, and a packaging strategy that fits major structural components within a 1.10-m diameter central core. Numerical modeling and small-scale prototypes confirmed a successful deployment sequence driven by a central telescopic jack and sliding joints.

# Review of research into bioregenerative life support system(s) which can support humans living in space

**Journal:** Life Sciences in Space Research 31 (2021) 113–120
**Authors:** Hong Liu, Zhikai Yao, Yuming Fu, Jiajie Feng

## Abstract
To travel beyond the Earth and realize long-term survival in deep space, humans need to construct Bioregenerative Life Support Systems (BLSS), which reduce the requirement for supplies from Earth by in situ regenerating oxygen, water, and food, and preventing pollution by recycling waste. Since the 1960s, the USSR/Russia, the United States, Europe, Japan, and China have carried out numerous studies in BLSS systematic theories, unit technologies, design/construction, and long-term operation. China's "Lunar Palace 365" experiment realized Earth-based closed human survival for a year with a material closure of >98%. Future BLSS research will focus on lunar probe payloads to study the impact of space environmental conditions on the ecosystem, providing theoretical and technological support for crewed deep space exploration.

## 1. Introduction
BLSS is an artificial closed ecosystem composed of humans, plants, animals, and microorganisms based on ecological principles. It combines biotechnology and engineering control to recycle and regenerate oxygen, water, food, and other essential substances. It is a key technology for crewed deep-space exploration, supporting long-term autonomous existence.

## 2. BLSS's theoretical and technological system framework
The framework is multidisciplinary, including biology, environmental engineering, ecology, nutrition, and materials science. The development path involves studying individual units, followed by artificial ecosystem technologies, design/construction methods, and finally experimental research with human participation.

## 3. Research progress of earth-based BLSS

### 3.1 Earth-based BLSS research: the Soviet Union/Russia
*   **BIOS-3:** A 315 m³ system with four compartments. It carried out crewed experiments for 4–6 months, achieving >90% closure in gas and water and meeting 40–45% of food needs for three people. In some experiments, 95% closure was reached.

### 3.2 Earth-based BLSS research: the United States
*   **NASA CELSS/ALS:** Developed for lunar and Martian bases. Experiments concluded that 43 m² of higher plant cultivation can provide 90% of a person's nutritional requirements.
*   **LMLSTP:** Integrated biological and physical/chemical technologies; the third stage achieved four-person closed survival for 91 days.
*   **Biosphere 2:** The largest closed ecological system (1.3 hectares). While the first experiment faced carbon-dioxide absorption issues into unsealed concrete, the second achieved 100% food production.

### 3.3 Earth-based BLSS research: Japan
*   **CEEF:** Introduced the first animal unit (goats). It used physical and chemical equipment for rapid circulation, though it largely ignored the role of microorganisms.

### 3.4 Earth-based BLSS research: Europe
*   **MELiSSA:** Managed by ESA, focusing on a five-compartment cycle (waste decomposition, nitrification, photosynthetic food production, and crew).
*   **DLR Lunar Greenhouse:** Studied optimal structural design using rigid-inflatable hybrid structures (semi-cylindrical, 20 m length, 3 m radius).

### 3.5 Earth-based BLSS research: China
*   **Lunar Palace 1:** A 500 m³ facility. The "Lunar Palace 365" experiment (2017-2018) involved four crew members for 370 days. It achieved 100% oxygen/water regeneration, 83% food regeneration, and an overall material closure of 98.2%.

## 4. Prospect of spatial BLSS experimental research
Experiments must move from Earth to extraterrestrial environments (Moon/Mars) to account for gravity, magnetic fields, and radiation. The Moon is the most suitable initial body, specifically the polar regions due to continuous illumination and potential water ice. In-situ resources (lunar soil) should be studied for utilization in large-scale closed ecosystems.

## 5. Development path and evaluation indices
**Three-stage Strategy:**
1.  **First Stage:** Hydroponics and processing in situ resources (lunar/Martian soil) with waste to prepare soil-like substrates.
2.  **Second Stage:** Expansion to large-scale soil-like substrate cultivation, including insects (mealworms) for animal protein.
3.  **Third Stage:** Complete cycling of inorganic salts and organic waste, utilizing artificial oceans for fish cultivation.

**Three Key Conditions for Gas Balance (Corrected):**
1.  If all food comes from internal biosynthesis, oxygen production is sufficient for breathing.
2.  Organic matter input from outside must be balanced by organic matter output of the same respiration quotient synthesized inside.
3.  Gas balance requires human intervention and cannot be achieved by biological self-organization alone.

## 6. Overall prospect
Future development will integrate lightweight, automated, real-time, and modular designs, utilizing nanotechnology, plant probiotics, and in situ resources to minimize transportation costs and environmental disturbance.
papers.keyFindings: Bioregenerative Life Support Systems (BLSS) have evolved from small algae cultivators to large-scale facilities like Lunar Palace 1, which achieved 98.2% material closure over 370 days. The paper proposes a three-stage strategy for extraterrestrial application, emphasizing the transition from Earth-based simulations to the use of in-situ lunar/Martian soil for preparing cultivation substrates (ISRU). Future construction must focus on modular, automated, and lightweight designs suitable for extreme lunar and Martian surface conditions.
papers.findings: A comprehensive review of the historical development of BLSS across major space agencies (USSR/Russia, NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CNSA). It identifies the transition from physical/chemical life support to biological regeneration as essential for deep space exploration and outlines the critical need for space-based calibration of Earth-based ecosystem models.
papers.result: The Lunar Palace 365 experiment demonstrated 100% regeneration of oxygen and water, 83% regeneration of food, and a 98.2% overall material closure rate for a 4-person crew. Structural modeling for a lunar greenhouse suggested a rigid-inflatable hybrid design (20m length, 3m radius) can yield 22 kg/month of dry edible biomass.

papers.title: Building Information Modeling (BIM) Workflows for Construction Sequencing & 4D-Planning of 3D-Printed ISRU Surface Habitats
papers.relevanceReason: The paper focuses on the development of BIM (Building Information Modeling) and 4D-planning workflows for the autonomous 3D printing of Mars surface habitats using in-situ resource utilization (ISRU).
papers.markdownContent:
# Building Information Modeling (BIM) Workflows for Construction Sequencing & 4D-Planning of 3D-Printed ISRU Surface Habitats

**M. Yashar, P. Michealsen, B. Hammond, J. Alvizar, C. Ciardullo, M. Morris, R. Pailes-Friedman, G. Bell, R. Tucker, T. Shen, S. Austin, L. LeBlanc**

## ABSTRACT
Future autonomously constructed surface habitats on the Moon and Mars will leverage additive manufacturing technologies to create airtight and durable structures. BIM workflows present significant value in the design and engineering of space systems, particularly habitat facilities including pre-integrated hardware (ECLS, airlocks, suitports). In 2019, team SEArch+/Apis Cor won first place in Virtual Construction (BIM) Level 2 within NASA’s Phase 3 Challenge for a 3D-Printed Habitat on Mars. This paper defines the landscape of BIM use and simulation as it applies to robotic deployment of space habitats.

## INTRODUCTION
Future long-duration missions will benefit from robotic precursor missions that autonomously construct infrastructure prior to crew arrival. Construction sequences must consider site conditions, ISRU feedstock quantities, power access, and environmental resources. SEArch+/Apis Cor merged BIM workflows between Rhino/Grasshopper, Autodesk Revit, Navisworks, and proprietary slicer software to estimate completion time and material quantities.

### BIM for Manufacturing and 3D-Printing
BIM enables the conversion of 3D geometry into CNC codes (G-code) for additive deposition mechanisms. While BIM is widely used in terrestrial AEC for planning, its application for real-time automated data collection and construction progress detection is still maturing. For space habitats, BIM must represent simplified geometries for additive manufacturing and integrate material extrusion through machine- and tool-paths.

## NASA’s Centennial Challenge: Mars X-House
The SEArch+ / Apis Cor submission (Mars X-House) prioritized radiation shielding and human-centered design. The competition required:
- Pressure-retaining living space of at least 93 m².
- Supporting four astronauts for one year.
- 4D construction sequence simulating machinery, AM, and component emplacement (ECLS, airlocks).
- BIM model Level of Development (LOD) 200 for MEP/ECLSS and LOD 400 for structural components.

### Software Workflow
- **Rhino/Grasshopper:** Parametric modeling of the regolith structural shell.
- **Autodesk Revit:** Interior design and assignment of material-based families.
- **Navisworks:** 4D construction sequencing, assigning model elements to schedule activities and calculating durations based on printer trajectory speed.
- **BIM 360:** Cloud-based collaboration and clash detection.

## CONCLUSION
Successful autonomous construction requires robotically placing wall apertures, interior partitions, and structural reinforcement. 3D-printed structural prototypes from the NASA challenge demonstrate that BIM can coordinate 3D-printing systems, ISRU regolith machinery, and space robotics within a unified construction sequence. Future research must address real-time "Dynamic BIM" or Digital Twins to handle communication delays and site deviations on Mars.
papers.keyFindings: Building Information Modeling (BIM) and 4D simulation are essential for coordinating autonomous robotic construction of ISRU-based habitats. A multi-software workflow (Rhino, Revit, Navisworks) allows for precise integration of structural 3D printing with the installation of pre-fabricated subsystems like ECLSS and airlocks.
papers.findings: BIM workflows facilitate the transition from architectural design to robotic manufacturing (CAD to CAM) in extraterrestrial environments. The study demonstrates that 4D simulation is critical for mission architecture planning, enabling the management of material flow, robotic pathing, and construction sequencing for Class III habitats.
papers.result: The SEArch+/Apis Cor team successfully achieved 100% design completion (LOD 200-400) for a 93 m² Martian habitat, simulating a complete autonomous construction sequence involving two mobile 3D printers and multiple robotic platforms.

papers.title: Extraterrestrial Construction in Lunar and Martian Environments
papers.relevanceReason: The paper provides a detailed review of extraterrestrial construction materials, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) processing techniques like sintering and biocementation, and various habitat design concepts (rigid, inflatable, underground) for the Moon and Mars.
papers.markdownContent:
# Extraterrestrial Construction in Lunar and Martian Environments

**Authors:** M. Z. Naser and Qiushi Chen  
**Publication:** Earth and Space 2021, ASCE

## ABSTRACT
Space exploration and terraforming nearby planets have been fascinating concepts for the longest time. Nowadays, technological advancements in manufacturing, robotics, and propellants are thriving, it is only a matter of time before humans can start colonizing nearby moons and planets. In recognition of the 50th anniversary of the first manned lunar landing, NASA, together with the European Space Agency (ESA), revealed plans to establish a permanent human presence (habitats) on the Moon and Mars by 2040. In order to facilitate feasible and sustainable space exploration, such habitats are envisioned to be primarily built from lunar and Martian in-situ resources. This paper explores the suitability of construction materials derived from lunar and Martian regolith, along with terrestrial derivatives, for interplanetary construction. This paper also identifies key processing techniques suitable to produce extraterrestrial construction materials under alien environments (i.e., vacuum, low gravity, etc.) and showcases prominent design concepts for “space-resilient” habitats and colonies.

## LUNAR AND MARTIAN IN-SITU RESOURCES
A comprehensive analysis led by NASA on collected lunar soil and rocks showed the presence of substantial amounts of alumina, calcium oxide and silicate. Table 1 compares chemical contents between lunar basalt, Martian soil, Martian lava, and cement.

### Table 1: Chemical content of lunar and Martian samples (by percentage of total weight)
| Constituent | Lunar Basalt¹ | Lunar Basalt² | Martian Sample³ | Martian Lava⁴ | Cement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| SiO₂ | 45.03 | 37.79 | 44.7 | 44.48 | 20.13 |
| Al₂O₃ | 7.27 | 8.85 | 5.7 | 11.25 | 5.98 |
| FeO | 21.09 | 19.66 | - | 11.38 | - |
| Fe₂O₃ | - | - | 18.2 | 3 | 2.35 |
| MgO | 16.45 | 8.44 | 8.3 | 17.32 | 1.19 |
| CaO | 8.01 | 10.74 | 5.6 | 9.54 | 64.01 |
| K₂O | 0.06 | 0.05 | <0.3 | 0.4 | 0.77 |
| TiO₂ | 2.54 | 12.97 | 0.9 | - | 0.37 |
| SO₃ | - | - | 7.7 | - | - |
| Cl | - | - | 0.7 | - | - |

¹Apollo 12; ²Apollo 17; ³Chryse Planitia; ⁴Calculated composition

## EXTRATERRESTRIAL CONSTRUCTION MATERIALS
- **Concrete-like derivatives:** Sulfur concrete, geopolymer concrete, polymer concrete, and waterless concrete.
- **Metals:** Extraction of Aluminum (Al), Magnesium (Mg), Iron (Fe), and Titanium (Ti) from regolith.
- **Advanced materials:** Composites, shape memory materials, and self-healing/sensing materials.

## PROCESSING TECHNIQUES
- **Sintering:** Heating powder below its melting point using solar, microwave (2.45 GHz), or laser energy (reported at 2.12 J/mm²).
- **Cold-pressing:** Leveraging adhesive forces and montmorillonite minerals in regolith to transform material into a solid under pressure.
- **Biocementation (MICP):** Using microorganisms (e.g., *Haematococcus pluvialis*) to precipitate CaCO₃ as a binding agent, potentially Mars-compatible using atmospheric CO₂.

## CONCEPTS FOR HABITATS
1. **Rigid Habitats:** Designed for load actions without secondary systems; high mass and transportation volume.
2. **Inflatable Habitats:** High packing coefficient for shipping; unfolded and inflated via mechanical/automated processes.
3. **Underground Habitats:** Utilization of natural lava tubes to provide shielding and stable environments.
4. **Mobile Habitats:** Concepts involving groups of independent rovers to improve exploration range.
papers.keyFindings: In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) is essential for sustainable space habitats, using regolith for concrete-like derivatives and extracted metals. Key processing techniques include sintering (solar, microwave, laser), cold-pressing, and microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP). Habitat strategies vary from rigid and inflatable structures to utilizing natural lunar/Martian lava tubes.
papers.findings: The paper synthesizes research on the feasibility of extraterrestrial construction using indigenous resources, identifying the chemical suitability of regolith and the maturity of various processing technologies.
papers.result: Chemical analysis confirms high SiO2 (37-45%) and FeO (11-21%) in regolith; sintering methods can produce 0.1 mm layers at 1000°C; laser sintering success is noted at 2.12 J/mm².

papers.title: Pressurized Greenhouse: A Responsive Environment to Partial Gravity Conditions
papers.relevanceReason: The paper discusses the design and structural considerations of greenhouse modules for Mars and Moon surfaces, focusing on pressure-vessel requirements, inflatable structures, and human factors within habitat systems.

# Pressurized Greenhouse: A Responsive Environment to Partial Gravity Conditions

**Authors:** Mahsa Moghimi Esfandabadi, Olga Bannova, Ph.D.
**Affiliation:** Sasakawa International Center for Space Architecture (SICSA), University of Houston
**Publication:** Earth and Space 2021 (ASCE)

## Abstract
The greenhouse is a vital module for long-duration missions to support fresh nutrition. This paper discusses two concepts: a habitable greenhouse focused on human factors/psychology and an industrial greenhouse focused on maximum nutrition with low mass. A third 'hybrid' concept is introduced: the **Pre-Breathe Greenhouse**. This module accommodates a spectrum of pressure and gas levels, serving as an alternative to tight airlocks for EVA pre-breathing, while supporting plant growth. The design is evaluated using Figures of Merit (FOM).

## Introduction
Greenhouses are essential for Mars survival due to the inability to carry all food supplies. Current designs include:
1. **Industrial-scale:** Prioritizes efficiency and low-pressure environments.
2. **Habitable:** Prioritizes crew wellness with Earth-like pressure.

## Greenhouse Approaches

### Habitable Greenhouses
- Integrated into logistics/service modules.
- Operates at equal pressure to the habitat (10.2–14.7 psi / 70.2–101.3 kPa).
- Simplifies ECLSS by unifying systems.
- Provides psychological 'backyard' feeling (e.g., MINA project).

### Industrial Greenhouse Approach
- Aims for maximum crop yields; neglects cultural/psychological factors.
- Designed for low-pressure (hypobaria) to minimize resource and launch mass.
- **Technical Data:** 
    - Pressure under 60 kPa allows for SiO2 aerogel-based thermal insulation.
    - Changing from artificial to natural/hybrid lighting reduces inflatable mass by 32.5% (compared to 59.2 kPa systems) and 39.9% (compared to 30.0 kPa systems).
    - Low-pressure shell mass using hybrid lighting is only 50.1% of a high-pressure artificial lighting shell.

### The Middle Path: The Pre-Breathe Greenhouse
- Allows internal pressure to fluctuate (34.48 to 56.5 kPa).
- Acts as a transition zone/pre-breathing chamber for EVAs (purging nitrogen to prevent DCS).
- Reduces stress by allowing gardening/exercise during the required 2-4 hour pre-breathe period.

## Comparison Data

### Table 2: Total Spent Time in Greenhouse
| Scenario | Total Duration | Pressure Range (kPa) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3x2h EVA | 7:20 | 101.3 -> 56.5 -> 29.7 -> 101.3 |
| 1x8h EVA | 4:40 | 101.3 -> 56.5 -> 29.7 -> 101.3 |

### Table 3: Figure of Merit (FOM)
| FOM | Private Garden | Industrial Greenhouse | Pre-Breathe Greenhouse |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Nutrition Support | Low/Medium | High | High |
| Mission Duration | Short | Long/Settlement | Long |
| Resources | High | High | Medium |
| Functionality | Single Function | Single Function | Multi-Functional |
| Impact on Habitat | High | Low | Medium/Low |
| Area/Volume Util. | Not Efficient | Max Efficient | Efficient |

## Conclusions
The pre-breathe greenhouse approach offers maximum benefits by utilizing fewer resources than habitable designs while maintaining lower mission risk and higher psychological benefits than purely industrial designs. It provides 24/7 availability and multifunctional capabilities.
papers.keyFindings: The research proposes a hybrid 'Pre-Breathe Greenhouse' that functions as both a plant growth module and an EVA preparation chamber, operating at intermediate pressures (34.48-56.5 kPa). This design reduces the total launch mass of the inflatable shell by approximately 50% compared to high-pressure artificial lighting designs while significantly improving crew psychological well-being compared to standard airlock procedures.
papers.findings: Comparison of three distinct greenhouse architectures (Habitable, Industrial, and Pre-Breathe) based on mass, power, human factors, and mission duration viability.
papers.result: Natural/hybrid lighting reduces inflatable mass by 32.5% compared to high-pressure greenhouses; the proposed pre-breathe greenhouse architecture utilizes a pressure range of 34.48 to 56.5 kPa to accommodate operational transitions.

papers.title: Design and Analysis of 3D-Printable Thin-Shell Dome Structures for Extraterrestrial Habitation
papers.relevanceReason: The paper details the design, material properties (Marscrete), autonomous 3D-printing construction methods, and structural analysis of an ISRU-based Martian habitat, directly aligning with space architecture and automated construction research.
papers.markdownContent:
# Design and Analysis of 3D-Printable Thin-Shell Dome Structures for Extraterrestrial Habitation

**Authors:** Matthew Troemner, Elham Ramyar, Benton Johnson, and Gianluca Cusatis
**Affiliations:** Northwestern Univ.; Skidmore, Owings & Merrill LLP
**Publication:** Earth and Space 2021, ASCE

## Abstract
Extreme environmental conditions and novel construction techniques will dictate the form of any extraterrestrial habitat on Mars. This paper presents the design and analysis of a dome-shaped Martian habitat developed for NASA’s 3D-Printed Habitat Challenge. The structure features a composite hemispheric-parabolic dome optimized for 3D-printing on an inflatable pressure vessel using 'Marscrete'—a Martian concrete made from local regolith and sulfur. The study evaluates structural performance under wind, gravity, and meteorite impact loads.

## Design Basis
The primary drivers were constructability, usability, and functionality. To minimize overhanging regions and the need for supports, a hemispheric-parabolic dome was selected. The internal hemispherical form matches an underlying inflatable pressure vessel, which serves as both atmospheric control and a construction mold. The exterior parabolic form ensures that most external loads result in compressive stresses, suitable for the quasi-brittle Marscrete material. Mass optimization resulted in shell thicknesses ranging from 21 to 108 cm.

## Construction Method
1. **Site Preparation:** Autonomous rovers clear debris and prepare a shallow foundation.
2. **Foundation Printing:** An articulated arm-type 3D-printer prints the foundation.
3. **Deployment:** A collapsible dome pressure vessel is inflated on the foundation.
4. **3D-Printing:** The pressure vessel acts as a support backing. A novel printing scheme utilizes a crawler robot deployed at the apex by an articulated arm to circumnavigate and print layers from bottom to top.
5. **Finishing:** An oculus is affixed at the peak. The pressure vessel is slightly deflated to allow for independent thermal expansion.

## Environment and Loading
- **Gravity:** 3.71 m/s² (38% of Earth).
- **Wind Load:** Calculated as 9.79 Pa (conservative estimate at 70 mph), increased to 60.0 Pa for analysis to account for dust density.
- **Sand Buildup:** Static pressure load of 2,780 Pa applied to one half of the structure (0.5m depth at 1,500 kg/m³ density).
- **Meteorite Impact:** Risk assessed via Lattice Discrete Particle Model (LDPM) simulations.

## Load Analysis
Finite element analysis showed that under all typical load combinations (ASCE-7), the structure remains in the elastic region with deformations less than 1.0 mm. 

## Meteorite Impact Performance
Simulations identified a critical load threshold:
- **Critical Impact:** 7,390 grams mass at 6.29 km/sec velocity (surface-normal).
- **Entry Mass:** Corresponding atmospheric entry mass of approximately 12,022 grams.
- **Risk:** Probability of a hazardous impact during a one-year mission is approximately 6.9 × 10⁻⁹.

## Proposed Layout
The 93-square-meter layout is inspired by 'tiny house' designs and NASA HI-SEAS. It includes:
- A central round common area under a transparent oculus.
- Public sector: Kitchen, workspaces, laboratory.
- Private sector: Bedrooms and lavatory.
- Two entries: One personnel airlock and one docking port for the Multi-Mission Space Exploration Vehicle (MMSEV).

## Conclusions
The hemispheric-parabolic dome design successfully meets the requirements for a one-year Martian mission. The construction scheme eliminates the need for complex printed supports by using an inflatable backing, and the structural shell provides high performance under Martian loads and meteorite risks.
papers.keyFindings: The study demonstrates a feasible Martian habitat design using Marscrete (sulfur concrete) and a hybrid construction method involving an inflatable pressure vessel and a crawler-based 3D printer. The parabolic dome form is optimized for compressive stability, effectively handling Martian gravity, wind, and sand buildup while maintaining high resistance to meteorite impacts.
papers.findings: The researchers developed a structural design and construction sequence for a Class III habitat on Mars. They utilized finite element analysis and Lattice Discrete Particle Model simulations to validate the structural integrity of thin-shell domes against environmental and impact loads.

The design can withstand a 7.39 kg meteorite impact at 6.29 km/s, with a hazardous impact probability of 6.9e-9 per mission year.

# The Research Facility on the Moon

**Mikolaj S. Trus**
Graduate of the Architecture Studies, Cracow Univ. of Technology, Kraków, Poland.

## ABSTRACT
The research facility on the Moon is an experimental, structural design for space exploration. It was developed as the Student Master Thesis at Cracow University of Technology, Faculty of Architecture. The main goal was to introduce innovative extraterrestrial architecture. Modularity, multifunctionality, and simplicity of the concept were key objectives. It was crucial to ensure the safety of the lunar crew. The facility is formed from seven modules. The construction of each of them consists of repetitive, easy to transport components. Project is prepared to host twelve astronauts, but it is expected to expand in the future. This structural concept for lunar architecture is universal and could be useful in other, different circumstances.

## INTRODUCTION

### Concept
The idea of a crewed base on the Moon was born at the Cracow University of Technology in February 2019. Difficulties related to transport defined strict requirements regarding the mass, dimensions, and form. The Moon environment presents challenges including 1/6th gravity, lack of atmosphere, meteoroid impacts, solar radiation, and extreme temperature amplitudes.

## METHODS
1. **Hand drawing:** Focused on visual stimuli and initial concept brainstorming, leading to the selection of the spherical shape as most efficient.
2. **Virtual model:** Created in Blender 3D to control shape, scale, and modularity. Truncated icosahedrons were identified as the most useful modular unit.
3. **3D printing:** Used to verify results of virtual design through physical scale models (1:200).
4. **Technical drawings:** Produced detailed sections and floorplans using CAD to ensure functional interior design.

## RESULTS

### Construction
The project utilizes a rigid assembly system over inflatable structures due to higher predictability in altered gravity. The core module is a truncated icosahedron (12 regular pentagons, 20 regular hexagons) which is triangulated for structural integrity. A light rod construction system forms an exoskeleton reinforced with internal support bars. Every module can be divided into twenty repetitive curved triangular elements for transport.

### Protection
The protection system consists of a multilayer shell:
- **Internal layer:** 20 cm thick thermal insulation.
- **Vacuum layer:** 5 cm gap acting as a thermal insulator.
- **External layer:** 5 cm thick layer to absorb radiation and temperature differences.
- **Regolith layer:** The final step involves covering the structure with lunar regolith for radiation absorption and meteoroid protection.

### Function
The base consists of seven spherical modules in a circular arrangement (three high, three low, one central). The top modules serve as living areas for four astronauts each. The bottom modules include a dining/kitchen sector, a laboratory sector, and a physical activity/gym sector. The facility supports a crew of twelve.

## DISCUSSION
The concept differs from the Foster + Partners lunar project in its assembly method. While the Foster design uses inflatable domes with robotic regolith printing, this concept uses repetitive rigid components and a vacuum-insulated shell before regolith application. Both respond to transport constraints and the need for multi-layered protection.

## CONCLUSION
The research proves the potential of regular polyhedrons in extraterrestrial architecture. The structural concept is multipotential and can be adjusted to various environments. Transport issues are resolved through repetitive components, and the functional design remains flexible and adjustable.
papers.keyFindings: The study proposes a modular lunar base consisting of seven interconnected spherical modules derived from truncated icosahedron geometry. The design features a hybrid protection system combining a 30cm multi-layered vacuum-insulated shell with a secondary outer layer of lunar regolith.
papers.findings: Design analysis identified spherical forms as optimal for internal pressure distribution and volume-to-surface ratio. The research concluded that a rigid rod-based exoskeleton is more predictable than inflatable structures for lunar environments, and modular growth can be achieved through antiprism-shaped corridor connectors.
papers.result: Individual spherical modules measure 10.02m in diameter with an internal volume of 520m3, featuring a protective shell comprised of 20cm internal insulation, a 5cm vacuum gap, and a 5cm external layer. The 7-module complex supports a 12-person crew with specialized zones for living, research, and life support.

papers.title: Bearing capacity of surface circular footings on granular material under low gravity fields
papers.relevanceReason: The paper investigates the bearing capacity of foundations on planetary regolith under low gravity conditions (Moon and Mars), which is fundamental for the structural stability and construction planning of extraterrestrial habitats.
papers.markdownContent:
# Bearing capacity of surface circular footings on granular material under low gravity fields

**Journal:** Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering 13 (2021) 612–625

## Abstract
Low gravity fields have been simulated through magnetic acceleration to conduct experimental study on bearing capacity of circular footings on a type of crushable planetary regolith simulant, which has comparable density and particle size distribution of lunar soil. The load–settlement responses of surface spread footings are obtained by investigating the relative density, footing size and gravity effects. The results show that the nonlinear gravity effect is not negligible, related to stress condition, soil dilatancy and mobilised friction angle. A cone penetration test (CPT)-based method for prediction of bearing capacity is proposed, improving the design of shallow foundations on the Moon and Mars.

## 1. Introduction
Space exploration tends to progress towards the creation of lunar or Martian bases and human habitats. The stability of these structures is significantly dependent on the interaction between foundations and planetary regolith under low gravity fields (Moon ≈ 1.625 m/s², Mars ≈ 3.711 m/s²). Isolated bearing pads are typical foundations for spacecraft (e.g., Lunar Module). This study uses Geotechnical Magnetic Similitude-Gravity Model Testing (GMMT) to simulate accurate low gravity fields.

## 2. Methodology
### 2.1 Materials
*   **Simulant:** CUMT-1c (crushable planetary regolith simulant).
*   **Properties:** Specific gravity $G_s = 2.93$, mean particle size $d_{50} = 0.12$ mm, angle of repose $\approx 42^\circ$.
*   **Preparation:** Magnetic sensitivity achieved by mixing cement, iron oxide powder, and water.

### 2.2 Testing Apparatus (GMMT)
*   Uses magnetic acceleration in the opposite direction to Earth gravity to simulate reduced gravity levels ($0g$ to $1g$).
*   Testing container: 86 mm inner diameter.
*   Footing sizes: 10 mm, 15 mm, 20 mm diameter circular footings.

## 3. Results
### 3.1 Gravity and Size Effects
*   Ultimate bearing capacity ($q_{ult}$) and foundation stiffness ($k_i$) generally increase with footing size, relative density, and gravity level.
*   The nonlinear gravity effect is significant. For example, $q_{ult}$ on the Moon is approximately 72% of that on Earth for the same footing.
*   The reduction ratio on Mars is approximately 84% compared to Earth.

### 3.2 Influence Zones
*   The normalized influence zone increases with relative density and decreases with footing size.
*   Gravity's effect on the influence zone is non-negligible; higher $g$-levels increase the influence zone.

### 3.3 CPT-based Prediction
*   A correlation is established between $q_{ult}$ and shallow penetration stiffness from miniature CPTs.
*   Formula for foundation stiffness: $k_i/P_{ref} = C_1 D_r^{C_2} (B/d_{50})^{C_3} (\gamma B/P_{ref})^{C_4}$.

## 4. Conclusion
Gravity fields have significant nonlinear relations with foundation stiffness and ultimate bearing capacity. Relative density has a more dominant effect on the mobilized friction angle than the gravity-induced stress gradient. The proposed CPT-based method provides a reliable way to estimate bearing capacity without extensive soil property estimation uncertainties.
papers.keyFindings: Gravity effects on bearing capacity are nonlinear and significant, with foundations on the Moon and Mars retaining approximately 72% and 84% of their Earth-equivalent ultimate capacity, respectively. Relative density is a critical factor, as an increase in density from 59% to 70% can more than double the bearing capacity. The study successfully validated a Cone Penetration Test (CPT)-based prediction method for estimating foundation stability in low-gravity extraterrestrial environments.
papers.findings: The study concludes that gravity-induced stress gradients significantly influence the bearing capacity factor and soil dilatancy. It establishes that planetary regolith simulants like CUMT-1c can effectively model the geotechnical behavior of lunar and Martian soil when used with magnetic acceleration systems. A multivariate nonlinear regression model was developed to predict foundation stiffness and ultimate capacity based on relative density, footing width, and gravity level.
papers.result: The ultimate bearing capacity of a circular footing on the Moon (1/6g) is approximately 72% of its capacity on Earth (1g). Increasing soil relative density ($D_r$) from 59% to 70% results in a foundation stiffness and ultimate load increase of over 2.5 times. Power functions used for prediction identified the footing size effect exponent $b$ as approximately 0.681, aligning with existing terrestrial geotechnical standards.

papers.title: Off Earth Landing and Launch Pad Construction—A Critical Technology for Establishing a Long-Term Presence on Extraterrestrial Surfaces
papers.relevanceReason: The paper focuses on the construction of landing and launch pads (LLP) on extraterrestrial surfaces (Moon and Mars) using ISRU and automated construction techniques to mitigate plume-regolith interaction risks.
papers.markdownContent:
# Off Earth Landing and Launch Pad Construction—A Critical Technology for Establishing a Long-Term Presence on Extraterrestrial Surfaces

**Authors:** Nathan J. Gelino, Robert P. Mueller, Robert W. Moses, James G. Mantovani, Philip T. Metzger, Brad C. Buckles, and Laurent Sibille

**Abstract:** In 2017, Space Policy Directive–1 aimed to lead human return to the Moon. Long-term presence requires numerous landings/launches, causing erosion and high-velocity ejecta from engine plumes. Construction of reusable landing/launch pad (LLP) infrastructure mitigates these risks by providing a benign surface and protecting assets with blast barriers. This paper baselines the state-of-the-art (SOTA) for LLP construction technologies and establishes comparison metrics for future trade studies.

## Introduction
Terrestrial vertical landing operations (e.g., SpaceX VTVL) have expanded the infrastructure needed for Launch & Landing Complexes (LLC). Functionally equivalent LLCs must be developed for Moon/Mars missions to ensure safe operations and reasonable life cycle costs. This paper specifically addresses the technologies and methods for constructing the LLP and associated blast barriers.

## Preliminary Engineering Assessment
Large-scale landers (Human Landing System - HLS) require 100 kN thrust engines, compared to Apollo’s 16 kN. Research suggests erosion rate scales with thrust/mass; an HLS lander could displace 16 metric tons of regolith, creating ejecta that exceeds lunar escape velocity and damages nearby assets. Novel lander designs (e.g., Hercules) may mitigate this by placing engines at the top of the vehicle.

## State of the Art and Past Work
The current Technology Readiness Level (TRL) for LLP construction is approximately TRL-2. Key research examples include:
- **Sintered Basalt Pavers:** Swamp Works and PISCES (Hawaii, 2016) robotically constructed a pad from sintered basalt pavers. 
- **Soil Stabilization:** Van Susante and Metzger (2016) tested rock beds and pavers; loose regolith was found ineffective.
- **Lunar Concrete:** A pad using KOHLS-1 simulant and polymer binders was tested for compression strength (Lee, 2012).

## Trade Study Criteria
Table 1 summarizes criteria across three phases:
1. **Preparation and Staging Phase:** Up-mass, Difficulty of ISRU handling, Site prep effort, Surface asset reliance, Crew interaction, Robotics/Autonomy, Robustness, TRL, Power.
2. **Construction Phase:** Constructability, Versatility, Construction time, Verification of as-built performance.
3. **Operations and Maintenance Phase:** Performance as LLP surface, Expected life, Ease of repairability, Lifecycle cost.

## Landing/Launch Pad Concepts
Table 2 lists proposed LLP structure concepts:
- Minimal Preparation / Existing Topography
- Compacted Regolith / Bedrock / Ice Surface
- Rock Piles
- Surface Stabilization (Polymers/Grids)
- Regolith Bags / Ice Bladders
- Pavers (Sintered, Polymer-bound, or Solar/Laser joined)
- Metallic Plates (Imported or Local Alloys)
- Deployable Structures (Mats/Blankets)
- Direct Emplacement: Sintered Structures (Solar/Laser), Polymer Concrete, or Hydraulic Concrete Pads.

## Conclusion
LLP infrastructure is necessary to reduce mission risk and facilitate the utilization of off-Earth resources. This paper provides the baseline for developing these critical technologies as NASA moves toward sustainable lunar exploration by 2028.
papers.keyFindings: Landing and launch pads are essential for mitigating high-velocity lunar regolith ejecta (over 2,000 m/s) which can damage both surface and orbital assets. Current construction technologies for these pads are at a low maturity level (TRL-2), requiring a standardized trade study framework to evaluate 14 distinct construction concepts ranging from minimal site preparation to advanced ISRU-based sintering and concrete emplacement.
papers.findings: The paper identifies that plume-regolith interactions for heavy landers (HLS class) can displace up to 16 tons of regolith per landing. It establishes a comprehensive list of 14 LLP construction concepts and proposes a robust evaluation framework based on 21 specific criteria across the preparation, construction, and operational phases of infrastructure development.
papers.result: Categorization of 14 landing pad structure concepts (e.g., sintered pavers, polymer concretes, deployable mats) and identification of significant technology gaps, particularly in the need for prototyping and testing under simulated lunar environments (thermal vacuum, UV, reduced gravity).

papers.title: Design of an Autonomously Deployable Mars Habitat
papers.relevanceReason: The paper presents a detailed design for a deployable Mars habitat that integrates inflatable and rigid structures with autonomous deployment mechanisms and utilizes in-situ regolith for radiation shielding.
papers.markdownContent:
# Design of an Autonomously Deployable Mars Habitat

**Authors:** Rudolf Walther Erdem Neumerkel, Miruna Vecerdi, Sandra Häuplik-Meusburger  
**Publication:** 50th International Conference on Environmental Systems (ICES-2021-398)  
**Date:** 12-15 July 2021

## Abstract
This paper presents a proposal for the design of an autonomously deployable habitat for a long-duration manned mission on Mars. Key drivers in the design were the payload and volume constraints of Starship and addressing habitability challenges implied by Martian conditions. The habitat is conceived to be transported in compacted form and to expand to a habitable volume by autonomously deploying after being placed on the Martian surface. The integration of several different kinetic structures is proposed: a protective casing, a vertically sliding core, radially expanding girders, and an inflatable membrane.

## Design Method
The design focuses on an integrated deployment mechanism fulfilling transportation constraints. The system consists of:
1.  **Protective Casing:** A rigid shell divided into 3 identical parts that interlock during transport.
2.  **Telescopic Core:** The primary rigid structure containing water/waste management and technical units. It features a water-filled cupola for natural lighting and radiation protection.
3.  **Expanding Girders:** Radially oriented foldable girders that push the casing elements outward using torsional and compressive springs.
4.  **Inflatable Membrane:** A multi-layered system adapted from TransHab concepts.

### Membrane Configuration
- **Interior Layer:** Nomex finish, redundant air bladders (CepacHD200), and Kevlar felt layers.
- **Middle Part:** Restraint layer of woven Kevlar belts.
- **Outer Layer:** Dust protection and a fillable chamber layer for loose regolith (up to 100cm thick).

## Technical Specifications

### Mass Estimation (Table 1 Summary)
| Component | Material | Volume (m³) | Density (kg/m³) | Mass (kg) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Core Frame | Aluminium | 0.26 | 2740 | 712.40 |
| Cupola Structure/Glass | Al/Glass | 0.50 | - | 1334.20 |
| Watertank | PE | 0.16 | 940 | 150.40 |
| Girders | Titanium | 0.25 | 4506 | 1126.50 |
| Floor | PE | 3.05 | 940 | 2867.00 |
| Casing Shell/Plates | Aluminium | 2.72 | 2740 | 7452.80 |
| Membrane Layers | Kevlar/Nomex | 5.78 | - | 7335.09 |
| **TOTAL** | | | | **27,988.53** |

### Volume and Expandability
- **Stowed Volume:** ~180 m³
- **Deployed Pressurized Volume:** 921 m³
- **Expandability Factor:** ~5
- **Planned Crew:** 4-6 members

## Arrival and Deployment
The Starship vehicle can transport two stacked units. Deployment steps include:
1. Casing elements unlock.
2. Compressive springs release girders to push casing outwards.
3. Membrane inflates, building pressure to 1 bar.
4. Interior core frame slides vertically, doubling in height.
5. Robotic filling of the outer membrane chambers with ground-up regolith for radiation/MMOD protection.

## Conclusion
The design addresses transportation constraints and Martian environmental challenges (no atmosphere, radiation, MMOD). It proposes a modular, reconfigurable habitat that can be deployed quickly and protected using ISRU regolith filling rather than energy-intensive sintering.
papers.keyFindings: The study develops a hybrid rigid-inflatable habitat with an expandability factor of 5, specifically sized for the SpaceX Starship. It utilizes a robotic regolith-filling system for its outer membrane chambers to provide 100cm of radiation shielding as a low-energy alternative to 3D sintering.
papers.findings: Development of a kinetic deployment system combining telescopic cores and expanding girders. The use of regolith-filled membrane chambers is shown to be structurally supported by 1 bar of internal pressure, with dead weight accounting for only 7.8% of the internal load.
papers.result: A habitat design with a total mass of approximately 28 tonnes, providing 921 cubic meters of pressurized volume, capable of housing 4-6 crew members and fitting within the 100-tonne payload limit of the Starship launcher.

papers.path: Papers/2021 Robert L. Worley II, S.M.ASCE.pdf
papers.relevanceReason: The paper investigates the geotechnical properties (cohesion) of lunar and Martian regolith simulants (JSC-1A and GRC-3), which is essential for in situ resource utilization (ISRU) and structural design of habitats on the Moon and Mars.

# Investigation into Measuring Low Levels of Cohesion of Regolith Simulants

**Authors:** Robert L. Worley II, Laura Obregon, Lane Feldeisen, Brandon Nimberger, Colin Palmer, and Mandar M. Dewoolkar

**Affiliation:** College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences, Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Univ. of Vermont, Burlington, VT

## Abstract
Lunar and Martian regoliths are similar to terrestrial soils in that they appear granular but are expected to contain a small amount of cohesion. Cohesion in extraterrestrial regoliths poses challenges for future space operations such as in situ resource utilization (ISRU). This study evaluated two methods—vertical cut and simple direct shear testing—to assess their efficacy in measuring small amounts of cohesion in lunar simulants JSC-1A and GRC-3. Findings indicate that vertical cut testing cohesion estimates for JSC-1A at relative densities 0%–80% ranged between 0.115 and 0.971 kPa and for GRC-3 ranged between 0.190 and 1.872 kPa. Vertical cut testing provided monotonically increasing cohesion estimates with increased relative density, whereas simple direct shear testing did not establish a clear trend.

## Introduction
Understanding surface regolith properties is critical for landing, walking, and utilizing lunar resources for habitat development. Soil shear strength is expressed by the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion:

$$\tau_f = \sigma \tan \phi + c$$ (Eq. 1)

Where $\tau_f$ is shear stress at failure, $\sigma$ is normal stress, $\phi$ is the internal friction angle, and $c$ is cohesion. Cohesion in lunar regolith is estimated at 0.1-1.0 kPa, likely due to mechanical interlocking of irregular particles.

## Experimental Methods

### Materials
Two simulants were tested: 
1. **JSC-1A:** Similar to Apollo 14 mare basalt; glass-rich basaltic ash.
2. **GRC-3:** A cheaper alternative for vehicle terramechanics testing.

**Table 1. General Material Properties of JSC-1A and GRC-3 (He, 2010; Dewoolkar et al., 2018).**
| Lunar Simulant | D10* (mm) | D30* (mm) | D60* (mm) | Dr (max) | Dr (min) | USCS Classification | Internal Friction Angle $\phi$ (degrees) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| JSC-1A | 0.017 | 0.042 | 0.110 | 2.040 | 1.560 | SP-SM | 34.9-59.6 |
| GRC-3 | 0.021 | 0.075 | 0.210 | 1.939 | 1.520 | SM | 30.4-57.2 |

### Vertical Cut Test
Cohesion is determined based on the 'critical height' ($H_c$) at which an unsupported vertical slope fails. The relationship is expressed as:

$$c = \frac{1}{2} \gamma H_c$$ (Eq. 2)

Where $\gamma$ is the unit weight of soil.

### Simple Direct Shear Test
This device allows testing at small normal loads (0, 1, 2, 5, and 10 kPa). Shear stress at failure is:

$$\tau_f = \frac{F}{A_{CS}}$$ (Eq. 3)

## Results and Discussion

**Table 2. Dry Densities of Lunar Simulants JSC-1A and GRC-3.**
| Relative Density (%) | JSC-1A (g/cm³) | GRC-3 (g/cm³) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.560 | 1.520 |
| 20 | 1.637 | 1.589 |
| 40 | 1.722 | 1.664 |
| 60 | 1.816 | 1.746 |
| 80 | 1.922 | 1.838 |
| 100 | 2.040 | 1.939 |

**Table 3. Vertical cut testing critical heights of JSC-1A and GRC-3.**
| Lunar Simulant | Trial | 0% RD | 20% RD | 40% RD | 60% RD | 80% RD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| JSC-1A (cm) | Average | 1.47 | 2.17 | 3.37 | 4.90 | 10.10 |
| GRC-3 (cm) | Average | 2.50 | 2.80 | 3.80 | 8.63 | 20.37 |

**Table 4. Cohesion estimates (kPa) from vertical cut and simple direct shear testing.**
| Lunar Simulant | Test Type | 0% RD | 20% RD | 40% RD | 60% RD | 80% RD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| JSC-1A | Vertical Cut | 0.115 | 0.178 | 0.290 | 0.445 | 0.971 |
| JSC-1A | Simple Direct Shear | 0.396 | 0.722 | 0.413 | 0.546 | 0.582 |
| GRC-3 | Vertical Cut | 0.190 | 0.222 | 0.316 | 0.753 | 1.872 |
| GRC-3 | Simple Direct Shear | 0.214 | 0.282 | 0.169 | 0.174 | 0.463 |

## Conclusions
Vertical cut testing provided cohesion estimates for JSC-1A that matched previous research and Apollo model estimates. The results support the hypothesis that regolith cohesion increases with relative density due to mechanical interlocking. Vertical cut testing is preferred over simple direct shear for estimating low levels of cohesion in regolith simulants due to higher resolution and established trends.
papers.keyFindings: Vertical cut testing is a more reliable method for measuring the low levels of cohesion in regolith simulants compared to simple direct shear testing. Cohesion values for JSC-1A and GRC-3 increase monotonically with relative density, likely due to the mechanical interlocking of irregular particles.
papers.findings: Comparative analysis of vertical cut testing and simple direct shear testing for determining cohesion in lunar simulants JSC-1A and GRC-3 across various relative densities.
papers.result: Cohesion values determined via vertical cut testing for JSC-1A ranged from 0.115 to 0.971 kPa and for GRC-3 from 0.190 to 1.872 kPa as relative density increased from 0% to 80%.

papers.relevanceReason: The study investigates the use of in-vivo biological binders (Human Serum Albumin and urea) combined with Lunar and Martian regolith to create construction materials (ERBs) for space habitat construction using ISRU and additive manufacturing.

# Blood, sweat, and tears: extraterrestrial regolith biocomposites with in vivo binders

**Authors:** A.D. Roberts, D.R. Whittall, R. Breitling, E. Takano, J.J. Blaker, S. Hay, N.S. Scrutton  
**Journal:** Materials Today Bio 12 (2021) 100136  
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.mtbio.2021.100136

## Abstract
The high cost and significant time delay associated with delivering payloads to the Martian surface means that exploitation of resources in situ—including inorganic rock and dust (regolith), water deposits, and atmospheric gases—will be an important part of any crewed mission to the Red Planet. In this work, we explore the use of human serum albumin (HSA)—a common protein obtained from blood plasma—as a binder for simulated Lunar and Martian regolith to produce so-called ‘extraterrestrial regolith biocomposites (ERBs).’ Employing a simple fabrication strategy, HSA-based ERBs were produced and displayed compressive strengths as high as 25.0 MPa. For comparison, standard concrete typically has a compressive strength ranging between 20 and 32 MPa. The incorporation of urea—which could be extracted from the urine, sweat, or tears of astronauts—could further increase the compressive strength by over 300% in some instances, with the best-performing formulation having an average compressive strength of 39.7 MPa. Furthermore, we demonstrate that HSA-ERBs have the potential to be 3D-printed, opening up an interesting potential avenue for extraterrestrial construction using human-derived feedstocks.

## 1. Introduction
Early extraterrestrial colonies will likely exploit loose unconsolidated rock and dust (regolith) as a bulk material for radiation and meteor shielding. Mechanical stabilization is required to prevent erosion from high-velocity exhaust plumes or dust storms. Strongly bonded regolith could serve as cost-effective construction material for habitat expansion. While several 3D-printing technologies based on in situ regolith are under development, biological binders produced in vivo by astronauts offer a ready source of materials that avoids the mass of synthetic resin production equipment.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.1 ERB fabrication procedure
HSA was dissolved in DI water to produce a 30 wt% solution. Simulants LHS-1 (Lunar) and MGS-1 (Martian) were packed into syringes and infused with the HSA solution. Samples were heated to 65 °C overnight (20 h) to facilitate dehydration and hardening.

### 2.2 Uniaxial compression tests
Tested using an Instron 5569 following ASTM C39/C39M-20 standards. Samples were cylindrical (12.1 mm diameter, ~24-30 mm length).

## 3. Results
### 3.1 Relationship between HSA-regolith mass ratio and ERB compressive strength
A positive correlation was found between HSA concentration and ultimate compressive strength (UCS) up to 35 wt%. Beyond 35 wt%, viscosity impeded impregnation.

**Table 2: HSA-ERBs prepared with different HSA concentrations (LHS-1 and MGS-1)**
| Regolith type | HSA conc. (wt. %) | Binder-to regolith mass ratio (%) | UCS (MPa) | Elastic modulus (MPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MGS-1 | 15 | 3.1 ± 0.1 | 1.9 ± 0.3 | 431 ± 111.8 |
| MGS-1 | 30 | 8.8 ± 0.3 | 6.6 ± 1.8 | 1257 ± 390 |
| MGS-1 | 35 | 8.1 ± 0.3 | 9.3 ± 1.2 | 968 ± 390 |
| LHS-1 | 15 | 3.7 ± 0.2 | 6.1 ± 1.7 | 236 ± 94 |
| LHS-1 | 30 | 8.0 ± 0.3 | 12.3 ± 2.2 | 1673 ± 890 |
| LHS-1 | 35 | 8.6 ± 0.3 | 25.0 ± 3.1 | 1618 ± 479 |

### 3.2 Incorporating urea into the formulation
The addition of urea (up to 3 M) significantly increased the UCS. For LHS-1 with 30 wt% HSA, the UCS increased by 324% when 3 M urea was employed.

**Table 3: Summary of HSA-ERBs with urea**
| Regolith type | HSA conc. (wt. %) | Urea conc. (M) | UCS (MPa) | Elastic modulus (MPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MGS-1 | 30 | 3 | 11.9 ± 1.3 | 939 ± 508 |
| LHS-1 | 30 | 3 | 39.7 ± 3.9 | 1746 ± 354 |
| LHS-1 | 35 | 2 | 37.4 ± 2.2 | 1823 ± 627 |

### 3.3 3D-printing potential
A simple scoping experiment demonstrated that a mixture of MGS-1 and HSA 15 wt% could be manually extruded to build layered structures. A 3D-printed structure (25x25mm, ~2cm height) sustained a force of 600 N.

## 4. Discussion and Conclusions
HSA-ERBs achieve compressive strengths comparable to standard concrete (20-32 MPa). Calculations suggest one astronaut could produce enough HSA to construct 2.5 kg of ERB per month, roughly one standard brick. Using urea enhances strength and potentially radiation shielding. HSA-ERBs are fully recyclable via dissolution.
papers.keyFindings: Human Serum Albumin (HSA) acts as a highly effective binder for Lunar and Martian regolith, achieving compressive strengths of 25 MPa. The addition of urea, another in-vivo resource, enhances this strength up to 39.7 MPa, surpassing standard terrestrial concrete. The study also demonstrates the potential for these biocomposites to be used in extrusion-based 3D printing for habitat construction.
papers.findings: The research identified that biological binders derived from crew members (HSA and urea) can mechanically stabilize extraterrestrial regolith. The adhesion mechanism is driven by dehydration-induced reorganization of protein structures into hydrogen-bonded beta-sheet networks. The resulting materials are recyclable and potentially more mission-efficient than transporting synthetic binders from Earth.
papers.result: Maximum compressive strength achieved was 39.7 MPa for LHS-1 regolith using 30% HSA and 3M urea. HSA-only biocomposites reached 25.0 MPa. A 3D-printed prototype sustained a 600 N force, equivalent to 162 kg on Mars.
